title: Practice Test 1: Claude Certified Architect Foundations
description:
60 unique scenario-based questions with another random selection of 4 out of 6 scenarios. Domain distribution matches official exam guide weightings. Topics include agentic loop implementation, MCP tool design, Claude Code configuration, structured output, and context window management.

As with the real exam, every question begins with a randomly selected scenario to frame it. These scenarios repeat, and that is expected.

Every question has been validated for technical accuracy and topic scope compliance. Detailed explanations with documentation references follow each question.

Prerequisite: Review the official exam guide and complete Anthropic's free certification preparation courses (or have equivalent hands-on experience).

SCENARIO: You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You need to integrate it into your development workflow with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and understand when to use plan mode vs direct execution.

QUESTION: This team keeps Terraform conventions that should load only while Claude edits files under terraform/, and it must guarantee that "terraform apply" never runs from a session. Which two steps achieve this? (Select TWO.)
answers: Save the conventions in ".claude/rules/terraform/" with no frontmatter, relying on the subdirectory to scope loading.
Add a "PreToolUse" hook in settings that blocks Bash commands containing "terraform apply".
Put the conventions and the apply ban in the root CLAUDE.md, marked IMPORTANT so they are reliably followed.
Create a ".claude/rules/" file with "paths: [\"terraform/**/*\"]" frontmatter containing the Terraform conventions.
feedbacks: Subdirectories under .claude/rules/ only help you organize files. Claude Code finds every Markdown file in that folder recursively. A rule without a paths field is loaded unconditionally at launch. So this file would act the same as always-on context. It would not load only for Terraform files.

Rules and CLAUDE.md are instructions that the model follows most of the time. They do not enforce anything. A PreToolUse hook runs as code before the tool executes, and it can block the call completely. This is the documented way to guarantee that an action never happens, no matter what the model decides.

The root CLAUDE.md loads into every session. So the Terraform conventions would use up context even when nobody is editing infrastructure. Emphasis words such as IMPORTANT raise the priority of an instruction only compared with the instructions around it. They cannot turn guidance into a guarantee. The apply ban would still depend on probabilistic compliance, which means the model is not guaranteed to follow it.

A rule file whose YAML frontmatter (the settings block at the top of the file) declares a paths glob loads only when Claude reads, writes, or edits a file that matches that pattern. This keeps the Terraform conventions out of context during unrelated work. The conventions are still applied automatically whenever Claude works on infrastructure files.
prompt.explanation:
Claude Code gives you two different kinds of mechanism, and the scenario needs one of each. Conditional conventions belong in .claude/rules/ with YAML frontmatter (the settings block at the top of the file). A file that begins with paths: ["terraform/**/*"] stays out of context until Claude reads, writes, or edits a file that matches that glob (or views one through a read-like Bash command such as cat). This is the purpose of path scoping: the conventions apply automatically when they are relevant, and they cost nothing when they are not. The directory structure under .claude/rules/ plays no part in this decision. Subfolders exist so that teams can organize many rule files. Any rule without a paths field is loaded unconditionally at launch, the same as CLAUDE.md content.

Hard prohibitions need a different mechanism, because rules and CLAUDE.md are instructions, not configuration. Every line in those files competes for the model's attention. Even a rule written in capitals is followed probabilistically, which means compliance is likely but not guaranteed. A PreToolUse hook, by contrast, is code that runs before the Bash tool executes. It can inspect the command and exit with a blocking status, so the call never happens. Permission deny rules give the same deterministic result for whole tools or command patterns. If a violation would only be annoying, write guidance. If a violation must be impossible, write a hook or a permission rule.

Putting everything into the root CLAUDE.md fails on both points. It loads the Terraform conventions into sessions that will never work on infrastructure, and this makes the rest of the file less effective. It also leaves the terraform apply ban as a request that the model could still ignore when other instructions compete with it. Documentation: Claude Code memory and rules, Hooks reference, and Permissions.

QUESTION: This team split its large CLAUDE.md into three files under ".claude/rules/" covering migrations, React components, and API handlers. Every session still loads all three at launch, even when only API code is being edited. What change makes each file load only when Claude works with matching files?
answers: Run /compact at the start of each session with instructions to keep only the relevant rules.
Move each rule file into a subdirectory of ".claude/rules/" named for the code area it covers.
Reference each rule file from the root CLAUDE.md with "@" imports instead of keeping them in ".claude/rules/".
Add YAML frontmatter with a "paths" field of glob patterns to each rule file.
feedbacks: Compaction summarizes conversation history after it has built up, and it can drop details. It is not a way to choose which rule files load. The rules would still be loaded at launch, and they could be reloaded later.

Claude Code finds rule files recursively, so subdirectories only help organize files. A rule in a subdirectory with no paths frontmatter (the settings block at the top of the file) still loads unconditionally at session start.

Imported files are expanded inline and loaded into context at launch. So imports organize content, but they do not reduce what is loaded. This would create the same always-on cost that the team is trying to remove.

A rule file under .claude/rules/ is loaded conditionally only when its frontmatter (the settings block at the top of the file) declares a paths field with glob patterns. Without that field, the rule is unscoped and loads at launch like the project-level CLAUDE.md. That is the behavior the team is seeing.
prompt.explanation:
Splitting one large CLAUDE.md into topic files under .claude/rules/ makes the instructions easier to maintain. But the split does not, by itself, change when those files enter context. A rule file with no frontmatter (the settings block at the top of the file) is unscoped: Claude Code loads it at session start with the same priority as the project CLAUDE.md. The conditional behavior appears only when a rule has YAML frontmatter with a paths field. This field can be a YAML list or a comma-separated string of glob patterns, such as src/api/**/* or **/*.test.tsx. Claude Code reads only that field from rule frontmatter and ignores any other keys.

Once a rule is path-scoped, it loads when Claude reads, writes, or edits a file that matches one of its patterns (or views a matching file through a read-like Bash command such as cat). This works as lazy loading based on file activity. The API conventions stay out of context during a session that only touches migrations, and they load as soon as Claude works with a handler file. For this reason, path-scoped rules are the recommended place for instructions that matter only in part of a codebase. Standards that apply everywhere stay in the root CLAUDE.md. Note one consequence: after compaction, path-scoped rules are reloaded on demand, not automatically re-injected like the root file. So a rule that must survive every compaction belongs in the root file, or its paths frontmatter should be removed.

The other approaches miss the mechanism. Subdirectories under .claude/rules/ are found recursively and only organize files. They do not scope anything. The @ import syntax keeps CLAUDE.md modular, but imported files are expanded and loaded at launch. So imports organize content without reducing context cost. Compaction summarizes history after the context has already filled, and it can lose exact details. It is a tool for managing long sessions, not a loader for instruction files. The documented benefit of path scoping is less noise and saved context space. Path-scoped rules are still instructional context, not enforcement, so hard constraints belong in hooks.

See Manage Claude's memory for rule frontmatter and load behavior, and Context window for how path-scoped rules behave around compaction.

QUESTION: A custom subagent runs the test suite during refactoring. When the suite times out partway, it reports only "tests could not be run", leaving the main session unable to decide what to do next. Which TWO reporting changes enable recovery? (Select TWO.)
answers: Have the subagent name the failure type and the exact command it attempted.
Have the subagent map every error to a single "tests unavailable" status for simpler handling.
Have the subagent report a passing result on timeout so the main session continues uninterrupted.
Have the subagent include results from tests that finished plus a suggested narrower rerun.
feedbacks: Naming the failure type (a timeout versus real test failures) and the command that was attempted gives the main session the information it needs. With it, the main session can choose between a retry, a different command, or going ahead. A timeout and a test suite with failing tests need very different next steps. A short "could not be run" message hides which one happened.

Putting all errors into one generic status is the same problem the team already has, only with different wording. It removes the failure type, the attempted command, and any partial progress. So the main session still cannot tell whether to retry, change approach, or stop.

Reporting success when the suite never finished is silent suppression: the failure is hidden from the main session. The main session would believe the refactor is verified when it is not. Failures must never be marked as successful, because the coordinator can make good decisions only with accurate information.

Partial results keep the work that was completed before the timeout. So the main session does not have to rerun everything or treat the whole run as unknown. A suggested alternative, such as rerunning only the module being refactored, gives the main session a concrete way to recover instead of leaving it to guess.
prompt.explanation:
In Claude Code, a subagent runs in its own isolated context. The parent session receives only the subagent's final report, not its intermediate tool calls or raw output. This design keeps long discovery and test output out of the main context window, and that is the reason the team delegated test runs. The tradeoff is that anything the subagent leaves out of its report is lost from the parent's point of view. A report that says only "tests could not be run" therefore removes everything the parent would need to recover.

An error report should carry enough structured context for the coordinator to choose between retrying, trying another approach, or going ahead with partial results. In practice, that means four things. The first is the failure type: a timeout is an access failure that calls for a decision about retrying, while failing assertions are a real finding. The second is what was attempted: the exact command, so that a retry can be adjusted instead of repeated unchanged. The third is partial results: tests that did complete still tell the parent something about the refactor. The fourth is possible alternatives, for example rerunning only the affected module or raising the timeout. The subagent may first try local recovery for a transient failure. But when it passes the problem up to the parent, it should include this context instead of a summary verdict.

The two incorrect approaches are both well-known anti-patterns. Reporting a pass on timeout is silent suppression: it turns a failure into a false fact that the parent will act on. In a refactoring workflow, that means merging changes that were not verified. Mapping every error to a single tests unavailable status is the generic status anti-pattern. It is easier to handle, but it throws away the distinctions that recovery depends on (timeout versus failure, full run versus partial run). Note that at the API level, the is_error flag on a tool_result is only a boolean. The detail needed for recovery has to be carried in the content or in a structured schema that you define. This is why the reporting instructions themselves matter so much.

See Agent SDK subagents for how context and results flow between parent and subagent, and Handle tool calls for how tool errors are reported to Claude.

QUESTION: A developer is several hours into a database migration session that has been compacted repeatedly. Claude now quotes the wrong migration version, port number, and agreed timeout, and the compacted summaries describe these only as "connection settings were discussed." What change most reliably fixes this?
answers: Keep the exact values in a structured facts file that Claude reads on every turn, outside the compacted history.
Run /compact less frequently so the session accumulates many more turns before any of the history is summarized.
Have Claude rate its confidence in each quoted value and ask you to confirm it whenever that confidence is low.
Give /compact a custom instruction to preserve every number and identifier verbatim in the summary it writes of older turns.
feedbacks: A structured facts block kept outside the summarized history is never compressed. So exact identifiers and numbers stay available, no matter how many times the session is compacted. Because Claude reads the file on each turn, the exact values are part of the working context. They do not depend on a lossy summary, which is a summary that loses detail, to carry them.

Compacting later only delays the moment when the exact values are condensed into vague text. It also lets long output make responses worse before compaction happens. The values are still lost once the summary is finally written.

Self-rated confidence is not a reliable measure of accuracy, because the model is often confident and wrong about details it no longer has in context. This option adds interruptions, but it does not restore the missing information that the answer depends on.

Custom compaction instructions can improve what a summary keeps. But a summary is still a probabilistic compression of history, so it is not guaranteed to keep every value, and it may drop or change one under pressure. This reduces the problem without removing the root cause: the exact facts exist only inside content that gets rewritten.
prompt.explanation:
This failure is the progressive summarization trap. Each time a long session is compacted, older turns are replaced with a summary that the model writes. Summaries naturally favor narrative over precision. "The team agreed on a 30 second timeout and migration 0047" becomes "connection settings were discussed." Once that happens, the exact values no longer exist anywhere in the context Claude sees. The model then fills the gap with guesses that look plausible. No amount of asking Claude to be careful can recover information that is not in the window.

The lasting fix is to treat transactional facts (versions, ports, timeouts, ticket numbers, dates, statuses) as curated state. Do not expect the conversation history to remember them for you. Write them into a structured facts file that Claude reads on every turn. This keeps them completely outside the summarized history. Compaction can then rewrite the narrative as much as it needs to, while the exact values stay intact. This matches Anthropic's guidance on three points: the context window is working memory that you should curate, structured formats should be used for tracking structured state, and you should not rely on summarization for details that a later turn needs. See Context windows and Compaction.

Customizing the compaction instruction is the most tempting alternative, because it acts at the right stage of the process. It is useful as a secondary measure. It is still a weaker mechanism, though. The summary is still generated text, and with enough history it can still drop or corrupt a value. So the facts are protected only probabilistically, not with a guarantee. Compacting less often only postpones the same loss, and in the meantime an overfull context makes responses worse. Confidence self-ratings do not help, because the model has no reliable signal that a value it is reconstructing is wrong. The fix must restore the information, not ask the model to estimate its own uncertainty. Anthropic's prompting guidance on structured state and clear delimiters is a useful reference when you design the facts file itself: Claude prompting best practices.

QUESTION: A developer asks Claude Code to implement a date-normalization helper with several tricky edge cases. Each time the developer describes a new failing case in words, Claude's fix breaks a case that worked before. Which workflow change best stops this cycle?
answers: Rewrite the request as a longer prose specification enumerating every edge case and expected result up front.
Switch to plan mode so Claude designs the helper's approach before it writes any code.
Run /compact after each round so earlier fixes stay in context and are not forgotten.
Have Claude write a test suite covering the edge cases first, then iterate on the failures until all pass.
feedbacks: A more detailed description still depends on Claude interpreting written descriptions consistently, and that is what has been failing. Without an executable check, nothing catches the moment when a fix for one case silently breaks another.

Plan mode is useful for large changes across many files, or when several architectural approaches compete. A single helper function with known edge cases does not need a design step before work starts. The problem in this scenario is verification during iteration, and planning does not provide that.

Compaction summarizes history to free context, and summarization can drop exact details such as the inputs of earlier cases. Even if the earlier fixes were remembered perfectly, the model would still have no way to confirm that they keep working after each change.

A test suite written before the implementation turns every edge case into a runnable check. So each iteration is judged against the full set of cases, not only the case that was just described. Sharing the failures from a run gives Claude concrete feedback that can be reproduced. A regression on an earlier case shows up immediately, instead of being found later in the conversation.
prompt.explanation:
Claude Code works in a loop: it gathers context, takes action, and verifies results. The verification step is only as strong as the check Claude is given to run. When the only feedback is the developer's written report of the latest broken input, Claude optimizes for that one case. It has no way to notice that an earlier case has regressed. Writing the tests first turns the whole set of edge cases into a single executable definition of done. Claude runs the suite, reads the failures, adjusts the implementation, and runs the suite again until everything passes. This is the test-driven iteration pattern that Anthropic recommends. The guidance includes asking Claude to create the tests before starting work and tracking their status in a structured file such as tests.json.

Sharing the actual failure output matters as much as having the tests. A pasted assertion error with the input and the expected and actual values has only one meaning. A sentence like "it still mishandles two-digit years" can be read in different ways. Concrete pairs of input and output, in tests or in examples, are the most reliable way to communicate a transformation rule.

Two cautions keep this workflow honest. First, Claude can focus too much on making tests pass. So the prompt should ask for a general solution that works for all valid inputs, and it should treat the suite as verification, not as the specification itself. Second, the prompt should state that removing or weakening a test to make the suite pass is not acceptable, because doing so hides missing or buggy behavior.

The other approaches address different problems. A longer specification in prose (ordinary sentences, not structured data) is still probabilistic guidance, so Claude is not guaranteed to follow it, and it gives no feedback loop. Plan mode is designed for large changes or changes with an unclear architecture, not for a single function with a clear scope. Running /compact manages context size and can lose exact details during summarization. It does nothing to detect regressions. See Claude Code Best Practices, Claude Prompting Best Practices, and Common Workflows.

QUESTION: A developer is adding "context: fork" to the team's skills. One skill, /license-audit, crawls every dependency and prints a long findings transcript before a short verdict. Another, /api-style, only lists conventions to follow while editing the current file. How should "context: fork" be set?
answers: Set "allowed-tools" on /license-audit to read-only tools so the audit produces a shorter transcript.
Set "context: fork" on /license-audit only and leave /api-style running inline in the main conversation.
Set "context: fork" on /api-style only, since its convention list is reference material rather than a task.
Set "context: fork" on both skills so that neither skill's content takes up space in the main conversation.
feedbacks: The allowed-tools field controls tool permissions during the turn in which the skill is invoked. It does not change how much the audit prints or where that output goes. The audit would still write its full transcript into the main conversation.

The license audit is an explicit task that produces a long transcript. Running it in a forked subagent keeps that output out of the main session and returns only the verdict. The conventions skill contains guidance, not a task, and it must be present where the editing happens. So it should run inline.

This reverses how the mechanism should be used. Reference material is the kind of content that should stay inline, so that it affects the edits Claude is making. The audit, with its long output, is the skill whose output needs to be isolated in a subagent.

A forked subagent receives the skill content as its prompt. It does not see the current conversation or the file being edited. Forking a skill that contains only conventions gives the subagent guidelines with no task to act on. So it returns little or nothing useful, and the conventions never reach the work in the main session.
prompt.explanation:
A skill is stored in SKILL.md under .claude/skills/NAME/. The older .claude/commands/ markdown files still work, but the skill format supports frontmatter (the settings block at the top of the file). By default, the body of a skill is injected into the current conversation when the skill is used. So everything the skill reads, runs, and prints builds up in the main context. Adding context: fork changes how the skill executes. Claude Code starts a new subagent and gives it the skill content as its prompt. Only the subagent's final result returns to the main conversation. The system prompt for that subagent comes from the agent field. This can be the built-in Explore, Plan, or general-purpose agent, or a custom subagent from .claude/agents/. If the field is omitted, general-purpose is used.

A forked skill is a delegated job, not a separate copy of the chat. Despite the name, the subagent does not receive the earlier conversation history. Built-in agents such as Explore and Plan also start without CLAUDE.md files, to keep their context small. This is why the fork is a good fit for /license-audit. The task is fully described in the skill, the crawl produces thousands of lines that nobody needs in the main session, and only the verdict comes back. The same property is why forking /api-style fails. A skill that only says "follow these conventions" gives the subagent no task to perform, and the subagent cannot see the file being edited. So the fork returns nothing useful, and the main session never sees the conventions. Guidance that should affect work in progress must load inline, where the edits are happening.

Two operational details matter when you adopt forks. First, in current versions, forked skills run in the background by default. This limits them to the background subagent tool set and keeps their edits outside the session's checkpoints. Setting background: false makes the caller wait and restores the full tool set. Second, allowed-tools is about permissions: it pre-approves the listed tools for the turn in which the skill is invoked. So it is not a setting for shrinking output or moving it somewhere else. The deciding judgment is to pick the skill that is a self-contained task with noisy output. See Claude Code Skills and Claude Code Subagents.

QUESTION: A developer on this team wrapped the internal code search service as an MCP tool for Claude Code. When the backend times out, the tool returns the same plain "no results" message it returns for queries that really match nothing, and Claude then concludes a helper does not exist and writes a duplicate. What change to the tool fixes this?
answers: Add a CLAUDE.md rule telling Claude to always re-run any search that comes back empty before it writes a new helper function.
Raise the tool's internal retry count on backend timeouts so that timeouts reach Claude less often.
Flag backend timeouts with "isError" true and a message saying the search timed out; return an empty list only for genuine no-match queries.
Attach a recent success-rate percentage for the search backend to every result so Claude can judge how trustworthy each empty answer is.
feedbacks: This instruction is probabilistic guidance added on top of a tool that still reports two different outcomes with one message. So Claude has no way to know which kind of empty answer it is looking at. The rule also doubles the cost of every legitimate empty search. And it still cannot tell a second timeout apart from a real absence.

Local retries are a reasonable first step for transient failures. But once the retries run out, the tool still turns the failure into a no-results message. The misleading signal is hidden more often, but it is not removed. The agent still cannot tell a failure from an absence.

A timeout and an empty set of matches are different facts. One says the search could not run. The other says the search ran and found nothing. Returning a flagged error whose content describes the timeout lets Claude decide to retry or ask before it writes code. A real empty list then stays a trustworthy signal that no helper exists.

An aggregate health metric describes the backend in general, not the specific call that just happened. So it cannot tell Claude whether this particular empty answer came from a timeout. The agent needs the outcome of the individual request, not a statistical estimate of it.
prompt.explanation:
A tool result is the only evidence an agent has about what happened on the other side of a call. Suppose a tool reports a backend timeout with the same text it uses for a legitimate empty set of matches. Then the agent cannot tell the search broke apart from the search found nothing. It reasonably takes the empty answer as a fact about the codebase. In this scenario, that false fact leads directly to duplicated helpers, because the model is doing what an empty search result should justify.

The documented way to signal a failed tool execution is a result flagged as an error, with content that describes what went wrong. For client and MCP tools, that means setting isError (or is_error in a raw tool_result) to true. The content should explain the failure, for example with a message that the search backend timed out. A tool may also use its own convention in structured output to hint whether a retry could work. But the contract that Claude relies on is the error flag plus the explanatory content. Claude uses that detail in its next step. It can retry a transient failure, narrow the query, or stop and ask the developer whether the helper already exists. Anthropic's own web search tool uses the same split. It returns an empty content list when a query succeeds with no matches. It returns a separate error object with a specific code when the search cannot run. This is done so that the two outcomes are never confused.

The other approaches all keep the single combined signal in place. A CLAUDE.md rule to re-run empty searches is guidance that the model may or may not follow. Even when Claude follows it, it cannot tell a second timeout apart from a real absence. Adding more internal retries is valid local recovery for transient errors. But a tool that still answers "no results" after its retries run out has only hidden the problem more often. A backend success-rate percentage is an aggregate about recent history. It gives no information about the one call that just returned, so it cannot resolve the ambiguity of the result Claude has.

The general principle is that generic statuses throw away the context that recovery decisions depend on. The consumer might be a developer's main session or a coordinator that receives a subagent report. In both cases, a result that says only "unavailable" or "no results" forces guesses. A flagged, descriptive error would allow an informed choice. See Handle tool calls for returning error results that Claude can act on, and Web search tool for how an empty result and a search error are represented differently.

QUESTION: This team's project CLAUDE.md states that Claude must never push directly to the main branch, yet in two sessions this month Claude pushed to main anyway. How should the team prevent this from recurring?
answers: Add a PostToolUse hook on Bash that detects pushes to main and reports the violation to Claude.
Add a PreToolUse hook that matches Bash and denies any push targeting the main branch.
Move the rule to the top of CLAUDE.md and mark it IMPORTANT so it gets priority.
Move the rule into an Agent Skill that loads whenever Claude works with git commands.
feedbacks: PostToolUse fires only after the tool call has already completed. So by the time the hook runs, the push to main has already happened. This event is a good fit for follow-up work, such as formatting or sending results back to Claude. But it cannot prevent an action that has already executed.

A PreToolUse hook runs after Claude has built the tool parameters and before the command executes. It can return a deny decision or exit code 2 to stop the call. The hook is a shell command that runs on every matching event. So the push is blocked whether or not Claude remembered the instruction or chose to follow it.

CLAUDE.md content is loaded as context that Claude follows as instructions. It is not enforced configuration. So emphasis makes compliance more likely, but it does not remove the chance of failure. The team has already seen the instruction skipped twice. This shows that stronger wording alone does not give the guarantee needed for a destructive action.

A skill is a procedure that Claude loads when its description matches the task. So the rule is still instruction text that Claude follows at its own discretion. It also applies only when the skill is actually triggered. And it does nothing to make the push impossible when Claude decides to run the command anyway.
prompt.explanation:
Claude Code gives a team two very different mechanisms for shaping behavior. CLAUDE.md and Agent Skills are both instructions. They are text that goes into the model's context, and Claude follows them the way it follows any other guidance. Anthropic's documentation states clearly that Claude treats these files as context, not as enforced configuration. It also states that every line in a memory file competes with every other line for attention. Compliance is therefore probabilistic: likely, but not guaranteed. A well-phrased rule in a prominent place will be followed most of the time. But "most of the time" is the failure the scenario describes: an instruction that worked in dozens of sessions was skipped in two.

Hooks are the other mechanism. A hook is a user-defined shell command that Claude Code runs automatically at a fixed point in the lifecycle. The behavior happens because the event fired, not because the model decided to do it. To stop an action before it occurs, the relevant event is PreToolUse. It runs after Claude has generated the tool parameters and before the tool executes. A hook matched to Bash can inspect the command. If it recognizes a push to main, it returns a deny permission decision (or exits with code 2), and the command never runs. This is the deterministic guarantee: the model can still try, but the harness refuses.

The two mechanisms do not compete; they answer different questions. Instructions are the right tool when you want nuance, judgment, and flexibility. Examples are coding conventions or a preferred testing style, where an occasional miss costs little and a hook would be too rigid. Hooks are the right tool for anything that must happen (or must never happen) every single time. This is especially true when a miss is hard to reverse, such as pushing to a protected branch, running a production migration, or deleting files outside the project. Choosing a prompt where a guarantee is required is a recognized anti-pattern, because the cost of the rare failure is greater than the convenience of the prompt.

Timing matters as much as the mechanism. This is why the PostToolUse approach falls short, even though it is a real hook. PostToolUse fires after a successful tool call. That makes it ideal for auto-formatting edited files or sending lint results back to Claude. But it cannot undo a push that has already reached the remote. Adding more emphasis in CLAUDE.md, or moving the rule into a skill, keeps the rule in the probabilistic category. In the skill case, the rule also applies only when the skill is actually triggered.

See Automate workflows with hooks for how hooks provide deterministic control and for PreToolUse examples, Hooks reference for decision control and the meaning of exit codes, and Manage Claude's memory for the statement that CLAUDE.md is context, not enforced configuration.

QUESTION: This team's monorepo has 14 service directories, each containing its own "migrations/" folder, and the same migration-authoring conventions should apply whenever Claude edits any migration file. Which configuration approach is most maintainable?
answers: Add the conventions to the root CLAUDE.md so they are present in every session regardless of task.
Add one rule file under ".claude/rules/" with a "paths" glob that matches every migrations directory.
Copy a migrations-specific CLAUDE.md into each service's migrations directory so it loads there.
Package the conventions as a skill in ".claude/skills/" that developers invoke on demand before editing migrations.
feedbacks: The root CLAUDE.md loads at launch in every session. So the migration conventions would take up context during frontend work, documentation tasks, and everything else. Instructions that matter only for part of the codebase belong in path-scoped rules. This keeps the always-loaded file short, and Claude follows a short file more reliably.

A single rule file with a paths glob, such as a pattern that matches any migrations folder, is kept in one central place. It loads only when Claude reads, writes, or edits a matching file. This gives one source of truth for a convention that applies in many separate directories. That is the case path-scoped rules are designed for.

Directory-level CLAUDE.md files do load on demand when Claude works in that subdirectory, so this would work. But it needs 14 copies of the same text. Every change to the convention must be copied to all of them, and over time the copies become different from each other. Per-directory files fit conventions that belong to one directory, not one rule that applies across the whole repository.

Skills package repeatable workflows and reference material. Claude can load them automatically when they are relevant, so they are not limited to manual use. But the content in this scenario is a convention that always applies, not a workflow. For guidance that always applies to separate paths in a large codebase, the documented mechanism is a path-scoped rule. Designing it as an on-demand skill adds a layer that a plain rule does not need.
prompt.explanation:
Claude Code offers two different ways to attach instructions to parts of a repository, and they answer two different questions. A subdirectory CLAUDE.md answers "what are the conventions of this folder?" It is stored next to the code, and it is loaded on demand when Claude reads, writes, or edits a file in that subtree. The owner of that directory naturally maintains it. A path-scoped rule under .claude/rules/ answers "what are the conventions for this kind of file, wherever it is?" It is a Markdown file whose YAML frontmatter (the settings block at the top of the file) has a paths list of glob patterns. It loads only when Claude works with a file that matches one of those globs.

Fourteen migrations folders that share one convention is the textbook case for the second mechanism. One rule file with a glob that matches any migrations directory is maintained in a single place. A change to the convention is a single edit, and the rule still loads only when Claude is actually working on a migration file. Copying a CLAUDE.md into every service folder would also load on demand. But it turns one convention into fourteen copies that must be kept in sync by hand, and in practice they become different. Anthropic's large-codebase guidance makes this same distinction. Use per-directory files when directory owners maintain local conventions. Use central path-scoped rules when the same rule applies to many separate paths.

The other two approaches fail for different reasons. Putting the conventions in the root CLAUDE.md loads them at launch in every session. There they compete for attention with everything else, even when no migration is involved. The guidance is to keep that file short and move instructions for part of the codebase into rules. Packaging the conventions as a skill is a mismatch of purpose, not a hard failure. Skills are packaged capabilities (repeatable workflows, procedures, reference material) that Claude can load automatically when they are relevant. But a few lines of convention that always applies are not a workflow. The feature comparison places language-specific or directory-specific guidelines under .claude/rules/, which is the mechanism that scopes to file paths. It keeps skills for on-demand workflows and reference material. Choosing a skill in this case adds structure that a plain rule does not need.

Two practical details are useful to remember. A rule file without a paths field is not path-specific. It loads unconditionally, with the same status as .claude/CLAUDE.md. The same happens if the frontmatter fails to parse. Also, neither rules nor CLAUDE.md enforce anything. They are context that Claude follows. So an action that must be blocked, no matter what Claude decides, belongs in a PreToolUse hook instead. See Manage Claude's memory, Working in large codebases, and Extend Claude Code.

QUESTION: The team's /sprint-summary command combines benchmark numbers, the rationale for a database migration, and dependency audit findings. Its prompt formats everything as bulleted lists, and reviewers find the benchmarks and migration rationale hard to follow. What should the team change?
answers: Specify per-section formats in the command prompt: a table for benchmarks, prose for the migration rationale, a list for audit findings.
Keep the single-list rule but mark it as IMPORTANT and add that every list must be easy to scan and complete.
Replace the list rule with an instruction to choose whichever layout reads best for each section, and leave the decision to Claude's judgment.
Split the command into three separate slash commands, one per content type, and have developers merge the outputs by hand.
feedbacks: Each content type has a natural format. Numeric comparisons are easiest to read as tables. Reasoning and narrative are easiest to read as prose (ordinary sentences, not structured data). Separate findings are easiest to read as structured lists. The prompt forced one uniform format onto all three sections. Stating the format for each section explicitly in the prompt is the direct fix.

Stronger wording cannot make a bulleted list a good way to compare benchmark numbers or to explain a migration decision with several steps. The problem is the uniform format itself, not how carefully the list is written. So emphasis alone leaves the readability problem in place.

This removes the harmful constraint, but it replaces it with a vague instruction. Anthropic's prompting guidance is to be specific about the output format you want. You should not assume that Claude will infer the right format from the content type alone. With this instruction, the results would vary from run to run.

Splitting the command adds manual work to combine the outputs. It also loses the convenience of a single summary, which is the reason the command exists. The formatting problem can be solved inside one prompt by naming the format for each section. So three commands add work that is not needed.
prompt.explanation:
When a summary output mixes several kinds of content, each kind should be shown in the format that suits it. Numeric comparisons, such as benchmark results, belong in a table, where columns line up and rows are easy to scan. Reasoning and narrative, such as the reasons for a migration, belong in prose (ordinary sentences, not structured data). A chain of trade-offs loses its logic when it is cut into fragments. Separate findings, such as audit results, belong in a structured list, where each item can be checked off. Forcing all three into bulleted lists is the uniform-format anti-pattern. It looks consistent on the page, but it makes two of the three sections harder to read.

Claude follows the formatting it is told to follow, so it should not be left to guess. Anthropic's Claude prompting best practices recommend being explicit about the output format. They also recommend detailed guidance on markdown, lists, and prose, and telling Claude what to do instead of what not to do. A per-section instruction in the .claude/commands/sprint-summary.md prompt (or in the newer Agent Skills form at .claude/skills/) does this with a single edit. A short example wrapped in an XML tag named example can make the layout even more consistent. The guardrail guidance on increasing output consistency makes the same point: specify the exact format you want, and constrain it with examples.

Telling Claude to pick whichever layout reads best is tempting, because it removes the bad constraint. But it replaces a wrong instruction with an instruction that does not say enough, so the format would change between runs. Adding emphasis to the existing list rule does nothing about the mismatch between content and format. Emphasis raises the priority of an instruction, but it does not fix a wrong instruction. Splitting the summary into three commands moves the work of combining the parts onto developers, when the fix is a few lines of prompt. Choosing the format for each content type is a prompt-design decision, and it should be stated explicitly in the summary prompt itself.

QUESTION: This team's monorepo keeps shared standards files in a top-level standards/ directory, and each package has its own CLAUDE.md owned by that package's maintainers, who know which standards apply to their code. How should each package's CLAUDE.md pick up only the standards that apply to it?
answers: Move every standards file's content into the root CLAUDE.md so that all packages inherit the complete set at launch.
Have each maintainer copy the full text of the applicable standards files into their package's CLAUDE.md so it is self-contained.
Ask the developers working on each package to add the applicable standards to their own ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md files.
Have each package's CLAUDE.md pull in only the applicable files with "@path" imports from the shared standards directory.
feedbacks: The root CLAUDE.md is loaded for every session in the repository. So this approach puts the API, frontend, and infrastructure standards into the context of every package, whether they are relevant or not. Longer always-loaded instructions use up context, and Claude follows each individual rule less reliably.

Copying the text gives each package the right standards at first, but it creates many copies that become different over time. When a shared standard changes, every package file must be updated by hand. The files that are missed silently stop matching the team convention.

A user-level CLAUDE.md applies to one person across all projects, and it is never shared through version control. Package standards would then depend on each developer's personal setup. New teammates would not receive them. The same file would also apply when the developer works in unrelated packages.

The @path import syntax lets a CLAUDE.md reference another file. That file is expanded into context at launch together with the file that imports it. Each package maintainer can choose the standards files that are relevant to their package. The standards themselves stay in one shared place under version control.
prompt.explanation:
Claude Code builds its instruction context from a hierarchy of CLAUDE.md files. There is the user-level file in the home directory, project-level files at the repository root, and directory-level files inside subdirectories. Files found in the working directory and its parent directories are combined at launch. A CLAUDE.md in a nested subdirectory is loaded on demand, once Claude starts reading or editing files there. In a monorepo, this means a per-package CLAUDE.md is the natural place for conventions that belong to that package's maintainers. Starting a session in one package does not pull the instructions of unrelated sibling packages into context.

The @path import syntax is what makes these per-package files modular. Writing @../../standards/api-conventions.md in packages/api/CLAUDE.md tells Claude Code to expand that standards file inline when the CLAUDE.md is loaded. Relative paths are resolved from the file that contains the import, not from the process working directory. So each package can point to the shared directory with a stable path. Nested imports are supported up to a limited depth. An import inside backticks or a fenced code block is treated as literal text, not as an import. The shared standards stay in one source under version control. Each package maintainer, who knows their area best, decides which standards to include.

Understand one limit: imports organize instructions, but they do not reduce their context cost, because imported content loads together with the file that references it. In this design, the savings come from where the imports are placed, not from the import itself. Each package imports only what applies to it. This is why moving every standard up into the root CLAUDE.md is the wrong direction: it makes every rule compete for attention in every session. Pasting the standards into each package file solves the selection problem. But it brings back the maintenance problem that shared files exist to avoid. A user-level CLAUDE.md is personal configuration, and it is never included with the repository.

See Manage Claude's memory for import syntax and load order, and Working with large codebases for per-package CLAUDE.md guidance in monorepos.

QUESTION: The project CLAUDE.md for this team now contains a 70-line step-by-step dependency upgrade procedure that developers run only a few times a month, and Claude has started overlooking shorter coding rules placed below it. How should the team reorganize this content?
answers: Keep the procedure in CLAUDE.md and prefix the coding rules with IMPORTANT so they are prioritized.
Move the upgrade procedure into a skill in .claude/skills/ and keep the coding rules in CLAUDE.md.
Move the procedure into each developer's ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md so the project file stays shorter.
Keep the procedure in CLAUDE.md but split it into a separate file pulled in with an "@path" import.
feedbacks: Emphasis markers raise priority only compared with the other content around them, and using them widely weakens their effect. The underlying problem is that a long procedure competes for attention in every session. Stronger wording does not remove it.

A procedure with many steps that is needed only occasionally is the kind of content a skill is designed for. A skill loads on demand when it is invoked, so the main context does not carry 70 lines of instructions during unrelated work. The coding rules that always apply stay in CLAUDE.md, where they load in every session. The shorter file also makes each remaining rule more likely to be followed.

User-level CLAUDE.md files are personal and are not shared through version control. So the team procedure would become different between developers, or be missing for new teammates. It would also still load in every session for each developer, so the context cost does not change.

Imports make CLAUDE.md better organized, but imported files are expanded inline at launch. So all 70 lines still load into every session. This does nothing to reduce the load on the context that is causing Claude to overlook the shorter rules.
prompt.explanation:
Claude Code gives teams two different places for instructions, and each is designed for a different kind of content. CLAUDE.md is loaded in full at the start of every session. This makes it the right place for facts and rules that Claude should always keep in mind: coding conventions, build commands, project structure, and short "always do X" or "never do Y" statements. The tradeoff is that every line in CLAUDE.md takes up context on every request and competes with every other line for attention. The longer the file, the less reliably Claude follows any single rule. A 70-line procedure in that file costs its full context on every session, even though it is relevant only a few times a month. The shorter rules below it are the ones that suffer.

A skill reverses that cost. Skills are directories under .claude/skills/ with a SKILL.md file. At session start, only their names and descriptions are loaded. The full body enters the conversation only when the skill is invoked. This happens when a developer types the slash command, or when Claude recognizes that the description is relevant. Anthropic's guidance says that some content should become a skill. One case is when a section of CLAUDE.md has grown from a fact into a procedure with many steps. Another is when you keep pasting the same checklist into chat. A dependency upgrade workflow is a textbook case. It is a repeatable sequence of steps, it is invoked on purpose, and it has no reason to affect sessions where the developer is fixing a bug or writing documentation. Checking the skill into the repository also keeps it shared with the whole team, which is the purpose of version-controlled .claude/ content.

Each alternative misses the actual mechanism. An @path import is a legitimate way to split a large CLAUDE.md into pieces that are easier to maintain. But imported files are expanded inline when the session launches. So the import changes where the text is stored, but not how much of it loads. Adding emphasis such as IMPORTANT to the coding rules treats a context-budget problem as a wording problem. Emphasis is only relative, and the procedure is still there, using up attention. Moving the procedure to ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md removes it from the shared project file, but it turns a team workflow into personal configuration that is not shared. The user-level file is also loaded in every session, so it does not reduce the load per session either.

The split is this: standards that are always relevant belong in CLAUDE.md, and procedures that are invoked or needed only occasionally belong in skills. Anything that must be enforced, not only followed, belongs in a hook. See Extend Claude Code for the side-by-side comparison, Skills for how skills load and are invoked, and Memory for what CLAUDE.md is intended to hold.

QUESTION: This team's documentation subagent in ".claude/agents/" has "tools: Write" only. It often stops to ask the main agent for function signatures. Once in a while, it also asks the main agent to run the test suite. Which TWO choices give the subagent the access it needs without giving it more than it needs? (Select TWO.)
answers: Keep the rare test-suite runs with the main agent instead of adding Bash to the subagent.
Remove the "tools" field so the subagent inherits every tool the main agent has.
Add Read and Grep to the subagent's "tools" list so it can look up signatures itself.
Add Bash to the subagent's "tools" list so it can search code and run the test suite itself.
feedbacks: Running the test suite is an occasional action with a bigger impact, and it is outside the documentation role. So it belongs with the coordinating agent, not in the subagent's toolset. Granting Bash for a rare need would give a general-purpose execution tool to an agent that will tend to misuse it.

Omitting the tools field does make the subagent inherit all available tools. But that replaces a toolset that is too narrow with one that is too large. Agents choose less reliably among many tools. A documentation writer that has Edit and Bash is likely to use them outside its specialization.

Signature lookups are frequent and low-risk. Granting narrow read-only tools removes the constant round trips without increasing the damage the subagent could do. Read and Grep let the subagent inspect code, but they add no command execution and no broad general-purpose tools. The existing Write access stays limited to producing documentation. This keeps the subagent inside its role.

Bash would let the subagent search code and run tests. But it gives a general-purpose execution tool to a documentation agent whose frequent need is read-only. Read and Grep cover the signature lookups without command execution, and the rare test runs can stay with the main agent.
prompt.explanation:
The core idea behind scoped cross-role tools is that a subagent's toolset should match how often it does something and how risky that action is. A documentation subagent writes files. But to document code accurately, it must check function signatures dozens of times per task. When only the main agent can do that lookup, every check becomes a full delegation round trip. This is slow, and it uses up the coordinator's context. Giving the subagent Read and Grep meets that frequent need with tools that cannot change anything. The subagent stays a reader of code and a writer of docs.

The other side of the pattern is just as important: rare capabilities with a bigger impact stay with the coordinator. Running the test suite requires Bash, which is a general-purpose execution tool, and the subagent needs it only occasionally. Adding it would give the documentation agent a tool outside its specialization. Agents that have tools they do not need tend to use them anyway. Sending those requests back through the main agent keeps execution in a place where it can be observed and controlled.

In Claude Code, this scoping is set directly in the subagent definition. The tools field in the frontmatter (the settings block at the top of the file) of a file under .claude/agents/ lists which tools that subagent sees. A tool that is not on the list does not exist in the subagent session at all; it is not blocked by a permission prompt. If the field is omitted, the subagent inherits every available tool. This is why removing the field is the over-correction to avoid. It replaces a toolset that is too narrow with one that is too wide, and the reliability of tool selection drops as the number of tools grows.

Pasting signatures into each delegation prompt might seem reasonable, because it follows the practice of passing context explicitly. But that practice fits one-time findings, not lookups that repeat. The coordinator would have to predict every symbol the documentation agent will need, and any miss brings back the original stall. A small read-only toolset solves the need at the interface level instead. See Subagents in the Agent SDK for how tool restrictions and inheritance work, and Claude prompting best practices for guidance on when work should stay with the orchestrating agent.

QUESTION: In the extraction pipeline described above, a custom "lookup_vendor" tool returns an empty result both when the vendor database times out and when no vendor matches the extracted name. Records are being finalized with blank vendor fields in both cases. What change should the tool make?
answers: Return a tool result with "is_error" set to true on timeout, and plain empty content when no vendor matches.
Have the model rate its confidence that the vendor exists and finalize the record only above a threshold.
Add a system prompt instruction telling Claude to ask a reviewer whenever the vendor field comes back empty.
Retry every empty lookup up to three times and treat the result as a genuine no-match only after that.
feedbacks: A timeout is an access failure that needs a decision about retrying. No matching vendor is a valid empty result, and that empty result is correct data. Signaling the failure explicitly through the error flag lets the orchestration layer and Claude react differently to each case. They no longer treat both cases as a missing vendor.

Self-rated confidence is not a reliable measure, and it has nothing to do with whether a database call timed out. The failure signal must come from the tool execution layer. It cannot come from the model guessing about an outcome it cannot observe.

When both empty results look the same, the model cannot tell whether the backend failed or the vendor really does not exist. A prompt instruction cannot restore information that the tool never provided. This option also sends every legitimate no-match case to a human, which wastes reviewer time.

Retrying every empty lookup still mixes up the two outcomes. A real no-match is retried for no reason, while an outage that is still happening after the retries ends up silently recorded as a missing vendor. Retries make sense only for transient failures, and that first requires the tool to say which outcome happened.
prompt.explanation:
The underlying problem is that two outcomes with different meanings are returned in the same form. One is an access failure: the vendor database timed out. The other is a valid empty result: the query ran successfully and matched nothing. Once both look the same, nothing later in the pipeline can recover the difference. The model, the validation layer, and the coordinator all see a missing vendor and finalize the record. The fix belongs at the source, in the tool itself.

The Messages API and the Agent SDK both give tools an explicit way to report this. A tool_result block can carry is_error: true to tell Claude that execution failed. Claude then takes that failure into account in its reasoning, instead of treating the content as ordinary data. An empty result is just as legitimate. A tool_result with no meaningful content and no error flag means that the tool ran and found nothing. Agent SDK custom tools offer the same contract through isError (TypeScript) or "is_error": True (Python). The documentation specifically recommends catching network and API failures and returning an error result with a message that says what to do. A raw exception or an empty payload should not be the only signal. The error flag answers "did the tool work?" The content answers "what did it find?" One signal must not answer both questions.

Here is why the other approaches fall short. Retrying every empty lookup treats correct data as suspicious. It also still lets an outage that is still happening after the retries be recorded as "no vendor" after the retries run out, because the tool never said which case it was. Move the overnight archive backlog to batch processing, since no one is waiting on those results.
Batch the real-time intake too, since most batches finish within an hour and the discount applies there as well.
Match each extraction result back to its source document by its position in the batch output file.
feedbacks: A batch can take up to 24 hours to finish, and there is no latency guarantee. So any consumer of the results must be able to accept that window. Deadlines that depend on batch output should be calculated backward from the 24-hour limit, not from typical completion times.

The archive backlog is a workload that can accept latency and does not block anyone. Batch processing is designed for this kind of workload. Moving it to batch gets the 50% discount without affecting anyone who is waiting for a response.

Most batches do complete within an hour. But that is a typical observation, not a guarantee. Processing can slow down when demand is high, or take up to 24 hours. A path where an operator is waiting cannot accept that uncertainty. So it belongs on the synchronous API, even though it loses the discount.

Batch results are not guaranteed to come back in the order they were submitted. So matching by position will silently pair extractions with the wrong documents. Each request carries a custom_id, and that identifier is the only reliable way to match a result with its source.
prompt.explanation:
The Message Batches API exists to accept more latency in return for lower cost. Requests are submitted together and processed asynchronously. They are billed at 50% of standard prices for both input and output tokens. The cost of that discount is time. Anthropic documents that most batches finish within an hour, but a batch may take up to 24 hours. Processing can slow down when demand is high, and there is no latency guarantee. Requests that are still not processed after 24 hours expire and are not billed. Think of batching as a queue: you put work into it and come back for the results later. It is not a slower version of the synchronous endpoint.

With that view, the workload decision becomes straightforward. Nobody is waiting on the overnight archive backlog, so it is a natural candidate for batching. This holds as long as its downstream consumers can accept the full processing window of up to 24 hours. Schedules should be planned backward from that maximum, not from typical completion times. The interactive intake path is the opposite. An operator is blocked until the extraction returns. A result that usually arrives in an hour but might arrive the next day is not acceptable. The most common way teams misuse batching is to reason from the typical completion time instead of the documented upper limit. Planning downstream deadlines around the full 24-hour window keeps integrations with other systems reliable.

Matching results to requests is the other way batching differs from synchronous calls. Results are delivered as a .jsonl file, and its lines are not guaranteed to follow the input order. So each request must carry a custom_id, and the consumer must join results on that field. For an extraction pipeline, this also makes failure handling simple. You find the few documents that errored or expired by their identifiers and resubmit only those, instead of reprocessing the whole batch. Select the content block whose "type" is "tool_use" and read its "input" object.
Instruct the model in the system prompt to emit no text before the JSON so the first block always parses.
Run a regex over the text block to isolate the JSON object before calling "JSON.parse".
feedbacks: Retries help with format or structural errors in generated output. They do not help when the parser reads the wrong part of the response. Repeating the call costs time and tokens, and it leaves the root cause in place: the code reads text instead of the tool_use input.

When Claude invokes an extraction tool, the structured data arrives as the input field of a tool_use content block. That data already has the shape of the input_schema. Going through the content blocks by type and reading input directly is the documented way to get it. This works whether or not a text block comes before the tool call.

A prompt instruction only lowers the chance of an introductory text block. It does not guarantee that the first block is the one that holds the data. More importantly, the extraction is in the input object of the tool_use block. So parsing any block as text reads the data from the wrong place, whatever the order of the blocks.

Regex extraction fixes a symptom by searching for JSON inside plain text. That kind of fragile parsing is what tool use is meant to remove. The data that matches the schema is already available as a parsed object in the tool_use block, so no text repair is needed.
prompt.explanation:
When you give Claude a tool whose input_schema describes the record you want, the model does not answer with JSON in plain text. It answers with a tool_use content block. This block carries an id, the tool name, and an input object, and the response's stop_reason is tool_use. The input object is the extraction. It already has the shape of the schema, and it is already parsed. So application code should go through the content array, select blocks by type, and read input from the tool_use block. Anthropic's guidance states clearly that code must not depend on a particular text layout. When tool_choice is auto, a response can legitimately contain a conversational text block before the tool call.

This is why the parser fails only some of the time, instead of every time. Sometimes the first block is text, and JSON.parse fails on English sentences. Sometimes the first block is the tool call itself, which has no text to parse. Neither case is fixed by prompting the model to skip the introduction, by pulling JSON out of plain text with a regex, or by retrying the same request. Those approaches treat the response as a text channel, but the data is delivered through a structured channel. Setting tool_choice to any, or forcing the named tool, does stop the introductory text. But the data still arrives in tool_use.input, so changing the parser is the real fix.

Two refinements complete the pattern in production. First, setting strict: true on the tool definition makes the API constrain sampling so that input strictly follows the schema. This removes the risk that a required field is omitted or has the wrong type. Second, a schema guarantees the shape of the data but not its meaning. So your code should still validate semantic rules downstream, such as totals that add up and dates in a plausible range. See Handle tool calls, Define tools, and Strict tool use.

QUESTION: An engineer on this team has used one long Agent SDK session to catalog layout variations across 200 sample invoices. They now want to try two competing extraction schema designs, each starting from that analysis without influencing the other. Which approach fits?
answers: Call "fork_session" on the baseline session and develop each schema design in its own fork.
Open two fresh sessions and paste a written summary of the layout catalog into each.
Resume the baseline session concurrently in two processes without forking and run one design in each.
Run both designs in sequence in the same session, telling the agent to disregard the first.
feedbacks: Forking copies the baseline transcript into a new session and leaves the original unchanged. So each fork receives the full invoice catalog, and then each one develops independently. Both schema experiments get the same starting point. Neither experiment affects the other, and the analysis does not need to be done again.

A hand-written summary is a lossy approximation of the baseline, which means it loses detail. Exact details found during cataloging, such as field variants and edge cases, can be dropped. It also requires setting up the baseline twice, while forking carries the complete analysis into both branches automatically.

Resuming without forking continues the same original session. So both experiments add their turns to one shared transcript. The two schema designs would see each other's work, and the experiments would no longer be independent.

A session cannot forget selected parts of its context on request. The first design's prompts, outputs, and tool results stay in the history, and they affect the second attempt. This is the contamination the engineer is trying to avoid.
prompt.explanation:
In the Claude Agent SDK, a session is a saved conversation transcript. Forking is the mechanism for taking one shared starting point and letting it split into separate paths. The Python fork_session() function copies the source session's transcript into a completely new session. It returns a ForkSessionResult whose session_id identifies the fork. You then pass that new ID as resume to continue the fork. The original session is not changed. So calling the function twice from the same baseline gives two independent branches. Each branch contains the full invoice-layout analysis up to the fork point. An optional up_to_message_id lets you branch from an earlier message instead of from the end of the transcript. The option-based form ClaudeAgentOptions(fork_session=True) creates the same split when you resume with resume.

The important point is that forking branches the conversation history, not the filesystem. A fork does not take a snapshot of files on disk, and it does not carry the original session's file checkpoints. If both branches edit schema files in the same working directory, those edits are real, and each branch can see the other's edits. For an extraction experiment, this usually means keeping each branch's schema in its own file or directory. If you need to revert disk state, use file checkpointing separately.

The alternatives fail for predictable reasons. Resuming the same session in two concurrent processes without forking does not create two histories. Both processes continue the one original transcript, so the turns of the two experiments mix and affect each other. Asking the agent to "disregard" the first attempt is an anti-pattern, because selected parts of context cannot be erased. Everything from the first design still affects the second. Pasting a summary into two fresh sessions loses the exact details of the catalog that took effort to find. It also repeats setup work that a fork provides at no cost.

See Agent SDK Sessions for the differences between continue, resume, and fork, the Python Agent SDK reference for the fork_session() signature and options, and File checkpointing for why transcript forks and file state are separate concerns.

QUESTION: In this system, the first-pass extraction stage sends each result to a reconciliation stage. Each result includes the full source passages and a long step-by-step reasoning narrative. The reconciliation stage has a tight context budget, and it now drops or misquotes fields. Which TWO changes address this? (Select TWO.)
answers: Remove the step-by-step reasoning field from the first-pass output and keep a per-field confidence score instead.
Move the reconciliation stage to a model with a larger context window and keep passing the full upstream output unchanged.
Define a JSON schema for the first-pass output containing extracted values, short evidence quotes, and page references.
Insert a prose summarization step that condenses each first-pass result before the reconciliation stage receives it.
feedbacks: For a downstream consumer, the reasoning narrative is the part of an upstream result that uses the most tokens and is the least useful. Anthropic's structured outputs guidance specifically warns against schema properties that ask for the model's step-by-step reasoning. A per-field confidence score gives the useful signal (how sure the extractor is) in a few tokens. It also makes it possible to send uncertain fields to review.

A larger window delays the failure but does not remove it. The long passages and reasoning still compete with the fields that matter, and recall gets worse as inputs get longer. The root cause is the shape of the upstream output, not the size of the downstream window.

A compact schema fixes the problem at the source, because it limits what the upstream stage outputs. The output contains the values themselves, a short supporting excerpt, and a reference to where each value was found. The reconciliation stage receives everything it needs to check a field and its source, without carrying whole passages. So its limited budget is spent on relevant data.

A free-text summary is lossy, which means it loses detail, and an extraction pipeline cannot accept this kind of loss. Summarization tends to make exact values, page references, and the link between a value and its evidence unclear. Another model pass also adds cost and latency, when the upstream stage could output compact structured data from the start.
prompt.explanation:
In a multi-stage extraction pipeline, the stage that uses another stage's output has its own context budget. Everything the upstream stage outputs goes into that budget. Claude's context window holds the system prompt, every message, every tool result, and the generated output. As the total grows, the model's accuracy and recall on specific items get worse (Context windows). When the upstream result carries whole source passages plus a reasoning narrative, the few fields that the reconciliation stage actually needs are a small part of what it must read. This is why values get dropped or misquoted.

The lasting fix is to change what is passed between stages. Have the first-pass stage return a compact structured artifact. It should contain the extracted values, a short evidence quote for each value, and a page or section reference. It should have a per-field confidence score instead of a narrative. The Structured outputs feature enforces such a schema through output_config.format with type: "json_schema". The same page warns against schema properties that ask for the model's step-by-step reasoning, because they can trigger a reasoning_extraction refusal. Reasoning is the right thing for the extractor to do while it works, but the wrong thing to send downstream. Note one limit: Anthropic's native citation blocks are not compatible with JSON structured outputs. So in this design, evidence quotes and page references are ordinary schema fields that the extractor fills in. They are not the API's built-in citations feature.

Each step in a pipeline should pass data, not transcripts. A bigger downstream window only delays the point where irrelevant tokens push out the relevant ones. An intermediate summary in prose (ordinary sentences, not structured data) makes the text shorter but loses detail, and it makes the exact numbers and locations that validation depends on unclear. Outputting structured data at the source keeps every step small and exact, and every value can be traced to its source. This lets later stages validate against the schema and send low-confidence fields to human review with the evidence attached.
