QUESTION: Reviewers for this system can manually check only one fifth of extracted documents. Today those documents are picked at random, so most field errors reach downstream systems unnoticed. How should the team decide which extractions get human review?
answers: Add a per-field confidence value to the extraction schema and route low-confidence extractions to reviewers.
Instruct the model to omit any field it is not highly confident about so only certain values ship downstream.
Add a validation-retry loop that resends schema errors to the model until every extraction passes validation.
Route the longest documents to reviewers, since lengthy source material produces the most extraction errors.
feedbacks: The model reports a confidence value next to each extracted field. This turns an untargeted random sample into a targeted one, because reviewer time goes to the fields that the model itself flagged as uncertain. The confidence is a field that the model produces. So the team should check it against a labeled sample and tune the routing threshold. Even so, it gives the downstream stage a usable signal that random sampling never provides.

Telling the model to be conservative reduces coverage instead of improving routing. Uncertain values that a reviewer could have corrected are dropped. Also, what the model considers "highly confident" still varies from document to document. Anthropic's guidance is the opposite: report everything with a confidence level, and let a separate stage decide what to filter or route.

A validation-retry loop fixes format and structural problems. But a document whose fields are all present and have the right types can still contain wrong values. Passing schema validation tells you nothing about which semantically incorrect extractions need a reviewer's attention. So this does not change how the one fifth is chosen.

Document length is an indirect measure that nobody has validated, and it ignores where the model actually had difficulty. A short but ambiguous invoice can have many more errors than a long, clearly structured contract. Routing on a rough guess like this, instead of a field-level signal, leaves most errors as hidden as random sampling did.
prompt.explanation:
The problem in this scenario is a routing problem, not an extraction problem. The system produces more output than humans can check, and the team needs a signal that shows which output is most likely wrong. The documented pattern is to separate coverage from filtering. The extraction step is asked to fill every field it can and to attach a confidence value to each one (and, where useful, a reason). A downstream stage, running in code, decides what to accept automatically and what to send to a person. Anthropic's code-review guidance makes this point directly. Asking the model to be conservative, or to report only what it is sure of, makes it report less. Asking it to report everything with a confidence level and filtering afterward keeps coverage and still lets you rank results. See Prompting Claude Opus 4.8.

In practice, the confidence is stored in the extraction schema as an ordinary field that the model writes. For example, it can be a number, or a small enum such as high, medium, or low, next to each extracted value. It is not a probability that the API computes. Structured outputs guarantee that the JSON parses and matches the schema. They do not guarantee that the values are correct or that the confidence is well calibrated, as Structured Outputs notes. For this reason, a competent team checks the results. It keeps a labeled sample and compares the stated confidence with the actual accuracy for each field. It then tunes the threshold so that the one fifth sent to reviewers contains most of the real errors. Stratified sampling of the automatically accepted documents then confirms that the threshold still works as the mix of documents changes. Grounding techniques make the confidence more honest. One example, described in Reduce hallucinations, is asking the model to quote the passage that supports a value. A value with no supporting quote is an obvious low-confidence candidate.

Each of the other approaches misses this. Instructing the model to omit uncertain fields moves the filtering into the extraction step, which is the anti-pattern the guidance warns against. Values that a reviewer could have fixed are silently lost. The model's own cutoff is no more consistent than the random sample it replaces. A validation-retry loop is useful for syntax and structural errors. But a document that is valid against the schema can still contain a wrong total or a wrong date, and passing validation gives the router nothing to rank on. Routing by document length uses a guess about error rates instead of a measured signal for each field. So reviewer effort is still spent without knowing where the model actually had difficulty.

QUESTION: Claude reviews a 16-file pull request to the extraction pipeline in a single pass. Comments are thorough on the document parsers, shallow on the schema validators, and a null-handling pattern is flagged in one file but accepted unchanged in another. How should this team restructure the review?
answers: Ask Claude to rate its confidence on each finding and discard those below a fixed threshold.
Run the single-pass review three times and keep only findings that appear in at least two runs.
Review each file separately for local issues, then run a distinct pass over cross-file data flows.
Move the review to a model with a larger context window so all 16 files fit comfortably.
feedbacks: Confidence or severity labels can help rank findings downstream. But filtering on them while the findings are being produced can hide useful results. It also does nothing about the files that got a shallow review, or about the contradictory verdicts on null handling. The review itself would still be a single pass with diluted attention, now with fewer visible results.

Repeating an unfocused pass does not make any single run more consistent. Real bugs that appear in only one run are thrown away by the agreement rule. This adds cost and hides findings, instead of fixing the reason the review is inconsistent.

Splitting the work into per-file passes gives every file its own focused, self-contained review. So each file gets the same depth of review. A single judgment, such as how null values are handled, is applied with the same explicit criteria each time. A separate integration pass then uses those per-file summaries and examines how the parsers, validators, and export module work together. This is what a single, overloaded pass misses.

Fitting the 16 files is not the problem described. The inconsistency comes from asking one general pass to apply the review criteria to everything at once. A larger window changes capacity but keeps the same structure. Nothing in it gives each file a focused, independent review, or adds a separate step for issues that span several files.
prompt.explanation:
The symptoms in this scenario are uneven depth, missed obvious issues, and the same pattern judged differently in two files. These are the classic signs of asking Claude to evaluate too many things in one general pass. When a single review must cover 16 files plus the review criteria, no structure guarantees that each file gets the same focused review. There is also no fixed reference point that keeps a verdict like null-handling is acceptable here consistent across all the files.

The pattern that fixes this is local first, then global. Each file (or small module) gets its own focused pass, which produces a short, structured list of local findings. A separate integration pass then takes those summaries and looks only at issues that span files. For example: do the parsers output the shape that the schema validators expect, and does the export module handle the validators' null conventions? In Claude Code, the natural building block for the per-file passes is a subagent. Anthropic documents that subagents run in their own context window, keep file contents and tool output out of the main conversation, and return only a summary. Non-fork subagents start fresh and do not see what the parent has read. So each per-file worker must be given its scope, the file paths, the review criteria, and the expected output format explicitly. Independent per-file passes can run in parallel. The documentation recommends starting multiple subagents for independent investigations and combining the results afterward. The integration pass belongs in the main conversation. The docs identify this as the right place when phases share a lot of context, such as the collected summaries.

The other approaches treat the symptom, not the cause. A larger context window changes capacity, not structure. The 16 files already fit, and the model would still have to weigh them in one pass with no separate cross-file step. Running the same single pass three times and keeping only findings that overlap throws away real bugs that happen to appear in only one run. Each run also stays just as inconsistent. Confidence labels are useful for ranking findings downstream. But applying a threshold to them while the findings are being produced hides results, and it does not improve the depth or consistency of the analysis behind them. Note that the per-file split has its own cost. Subagent requests count toward the same usage limits, and many detailed summaries still use main-context tokens. The team accepts this cost in return for consistent, trustworthy findings.

QUESTION: The extraction tool's schema declares "source" as a nullable string, and the instructions describe both citation styles. Some documents use a numbered bibliography instead of inline citations. For these documents, "source" always comes back null, even though the reference list contains it. What change most reliably fixes this?

Return every null "source" result to Claude with a validation error so it retries the extraction attempt.
Add few-shot examples demonstrating "source" extraction from inline-citation and bibliography-style documents.
Add an emphatic instruction stating that "source" must always be taken from the document's reference list.
feedbacks: Making the field strictly required changes the shape the output must take. It does not change what the model understands about the document. For documents where a source really is absent, a required field that cannot be null pushes the model to invent a value. A visible null is replaced by a silent fabrication.

Retry with error feedback works well for format and structural mistakes. But a plain retry gives no new guidance about where to look in a bibliography-style document, so the second attempt will probably repeat the first. Treating every null as an error also penalizes the legitimate case where the document really has no source, and this encourages guesses.

The model is not failing on syntax, and the data is not absent. The model fails to recognize where the value is in a document layout it does not know well. Contrasting examples show the same field being taken from an inline citation and from a numbered reference entry. They demonstrate the judgment that the written instructions did not communicate, and the model applies that pattern to new documents.

The prompt already describes both citation styles. Stronger wording adds emphasis, but it adds no practical information about how a numbered reference maps to an extracted value. An absolute rule about the reference list would also be wrong for inline-citation documents, which have no such list.
prompt.explanation:
When a field is clearly present in the source but the extraction returns it as empty or null, that is a recognition failure, not a schema failure. The schema describes the shape of the answer. It says nothing about how a value is laid out in different document conventions. In one document, a value may appear in parentheses inline. In another, it may appear as a numbered entry in a reference list. Written instructions can describe both conventions and still leave the model unsure how to connect a bracketed number in the text to the matching bibliography entry. In this situation, few-shot examples work better than more instructions. A few contrasting examples each show a document fragment and the correct extracted object. They demonstrate the mapping instead of describing it, and the model applies what it learns from them to new layouts.

Good examples for this problem are diverse: they cover the formats that actually appear in production. They are also relevant to the edge case being fixed. Each example should be wrapped in an XML tag named example, so that the model can tell demonstrations apart from instructions and from the target document. Anthropic's prompting best practices describe examples as one of the most reliable ways to control output structure. The same page recommends XML structure for separating documents, metadata, and examples in complex prompts.

Each alternative addresses a different problem. Removing null from the field's allowed types forces the model to output something for every document. For a bibliography-style document, the model still may not know which value to use. For a document with no source at all, the model is now pushed to invent one. Keeping fields nullable when the information may be absent is a deliberate schema design choice. It is covered in the Structured Outputs documentation and in the hallucination-reduction guidance, which recommends giving the model an honest way to report missing information. A validation-retry loop is the right tool when the model produced the wrong format or put a value in the wrong field, because the error message tells the model what to correct. A message that only says the field was null gives no new information about the document. It would also be triggered for documents where the field is legitimately empty. Emphatic wording about the reference list makes an existing instruction stronger. Stated as an absolute rule, it would be wrong for inline-citation documents.

QUESTION: Three extraction tools (one each for invoices, receipts, and purchase orders) are defined, and tool selection is left at its default. Assume the model and its settings support every "tool_choice" option. Documents arrive unlabeled, and about one in twenty responses is a short text description of the document instead of a tool call, which breaks the downstream parser. Which change ensures every document yields a structured extraction while Claude still picks the schema?
answers: Keep the default "tool_choice" and resubmit any document whose response arrives as text rather than a tool call.
Force "tool_choice" to the invoice extraction tool because invoices are the most common document type in the stream.
Keep the default "tool_choice" and strengthen the system prompt to insist that a tool is called for every document.

feedbacks: Retrying does not change the underlying behavior. So some of the retries will again produce text, and each retry adds latency and cost. A deterministic setting that prevents the text response is available. This makes a retry loop the wrong layer for this fix.

Forcing a named tool guarantees a tool call. But it forces every document into the invoice schema, whatever the document actually is. Receipts and purchase orders would be forced into the wrong fields. A parsing failure would be replaced by silent semantic errors.

Under the default "auto" setting, Claude is still free to answer in text. So a prompt instruction only makes a tool call more likely; it does not guarantee one. The documented way to require tool use is the tool_choice parameter, not stronger wording.

On a model that accepts forced tool use, the "any" setting requires Claude to call one of the provided tools. But it leaves the choice of which tool to the model. So unlabeled documents can still be routed to the matching schema. The API also prefills the assistant turn, so no explanatory text comes before the tool call. This removes the failure that the parser is hitting.
prompt.explanation:
The tool_choice parameter is how an application tells the Messages API whether a tool call is optional, required, or fixed to one tool. The default, {"type": "auto"}, lets Claude decide between calling a tool and replying in text. This is right for conversational assistants. It is wrong for an extraction pipeline whose parser expects a tool_use block every time. The occasional text reply in the scenario is not a bug in the prompt. It is the documented behavior of the default mode.

Setting {"type": "any"} changes the contract. Claude must use one of the provided tools, but it still chooses which one, based on the tool descriptions and the document content. This fits unlabeled documents with several possible schemas, because the model acts as both the classifier and the extractor in a single step. When a forced mode is active, the API prefills the assistant message. So the response starts directly with the tool call, not with an introduction in natural language. If the pipeline should receive exactly one extraction per document, disable_parallel_tool_use: true can be added inside tool_choice. Combined with any, that means exactly one tool call.

Forcing a named tool with {"type": "tool", "name": ...} is the right choice when a specific step must run first, such as extracting metadata before enrichment. But it removes the model's ability to match the schema to the document. Prompt wording and retry loops both work on probabilities. They can reduce the rate of text replies, but they cannot remove them, while a request-level setting can. Remember that guaranteeing a tool call is separate from guaranteeing that the input matches the schema. strict: true on the tool definition handles schema conformance of tool_use.input. Neither setting prevents semantic mistakes, such as a total that does not match its line items. The guarantee also depends on the model and settings. Not every model accepts forced tool use, and manual extended thinking rejects any and tool. The scenario states that the model accepts forced tool use with thinking disabled, and this is why any gives the guarantee in this case. Where a model instead returns a 400 error for any or tool, Anthropic recommends auto with strict tool use, or the structured outputs feature for a fixed JSON shape.

answers: Submit both workloads as batches and poll for completion every few seconds so upload users receive results promptly.
Keep both workloads synchronous and reduce the number of extracted fields per document to lower token usage.
Submit both workloads as batches, falling back to a synchronous call whenever a batch has not finished within a minute.
Submit the nightly archive backfill as batches and keep the interactive upload screen on synchronous Messages API calls.
feedbacks: How often you poll does not change how fast a batch is processed. The Message Batches API has no latency SLA, and a batch may take up to 24 hours. A user waiting on an upload screen cannot be served by a mechanism that may not return for many hours, however often the client checks.

Removing fields reduces output tokens a little. But it weakens the purpose of the extraction system itself, and the large nightly workload still pays full synchronous prices. The archive backfill is the kind of large, non-blocking job that the Message Batches API exists to make cheaper.

For the upload screen, this fallback would be triggered on almost every request. So the team pays for both the batch request and the synchronous call, and the user still waits a full minute first. It also adds branching logic that a simple split of the workloads avoids completely.

The nightly backfill is a large workload that can accept latency, and its results are needed only by morning. So it fits the asynchronous batch model and gets the 50% discount. On the upload screen, a user is waiting for results. Batch processing has no latency guarantee and can take up to 24 hours, so that path must stay synchronous.
prompt.explanation:
The Message Batches API is built around one trade-off. You give up control over when a request is processed, and in return you get a 50% price reduction. Requests are submitted as a group and processed asynchronously. They are returned as a single results file once every request has finished or the 24-hour window has passed. Anthropic notes that most batches finish in under an hour, but that is an observation, not a guarantee. There is no latency SLA, and a batch that does not complete within 24 hours expires. So the decision rule for an architect is simple: ask whether anyone or anything is blocked waiting for the result. If nothing is blocked, use a batch. If something is blocked, stay synchronous.

Applying that rule to the extraction system splits the two workloads clearly. The nightly backfill of 40,000 archived documents is large, scheduled work. Its consumer is a dashboard that is refreshed in the morning. So an overnight batch is a natural fit, and the cost savings are large because the volume is large. Each archived document should carry its own custom_id. Results are not guaranteed to come back in the order they were submitted. The ID lets the team match results to source documents and resubmit any errored or expired items one by one. The interactive upload screen is the opposite case. A person is on the page, waiting to confirm the extracted fields. A channel that may not respond for hours is the wrong tool, whatever workaround is added to it.

The other approaches all try to force the interactive path onto batch processing, or they avoid batching completely. Polling more often only asks the API more often whether the work is done. It does not make the work finish sooner. A timed fallback to synchronous calls would be triggered on almost every upload. This would double the cost on that path and still delay the user. Cutting extracted fields to save tokens reduces the product's value, and the expensive bulk workload still pays full synchronous rates. Matching each workload to the API whose latency it can accept is what gets the savings without making the user experience worse.

QUESTION: The validation-retry loop resends each invoice with its specific validation error. Date-format failures clear after one retry, but "vendor_tax_id" failures persist through three retries because that ID exists only in a separate vendor registry that is never sent to Claude. What should the team do for these failures?
answers: Add few-shot examples showing correctly extracted tax IDs from several differently structured invoices.
Stop retrying those invoices and include the matching vendor registry record in the extraction prompt.
Strengthen the retry instruction to state that the tax ID is mandatory and must never be left empty.
Raise the retry limit from three to six and include the prior incorrect extraction in each retry prompt.
feedbacks: Few-shot examples improve consistency and the handling of varied document layouts, when the information is present somewhere in the input. They do not help when the value is not in the invoice at all. So the extraction would still fail for the same reason.

Retry with feedback works when the model has the information but formatted it wrong or put it in the wrong place. It cannot work when the required value is absent from everything the model can see. Supplying the registry record (or a lookup tool) gives Claude the missing source. This is the only change that can turn these failures into successful extractions.

Stronger wording cannot create data that is absent from the document and the context. The likely result is an invented ID that passes schema validation but is wrong. For downstream systems, that is a worse failure than an honest empty field.

More attempts do not change what the model can see. An ID that is not in the prompt is still unavailable on the sixth retry, the same as on the first. Extra retries in this case only add cost and latency. They also increase the chance that the model finally invents a plausible-looking value to satisfy the validator.
prompt.explanation:
The validation-retry loop is built on a specific assumption: Claude produced a wrong answer from information it actually had. Suppose a date comes back as 03/14/2024 instead of ISO 8601, or a value ends up in the wrong field. Resending the document with the previous extraction and a concrete error message gives the model everything it needs to correct itself. One or two retries usually resolve such cases. The feedback works because it focuses the model's attention on a mistake that can be fixed from the existing input.

The vendor_tax_id failures that keep happening belong to a different class. The invoice never contained the ID. The ID is stored in a registry that was never part of the prompt. Retrying, stronger wording, and better examples do not change the information the model has. So the correct step is to stop retrying and supply the missing source. You can attach the registry record to the prompt, or you can provide a lookup tool that the model can call. This matches Anthropic's guidance: when the needed information is external, the fix is to provide context or tools, not to resend the same request. See Tool use overview.

The other approaches fail for related reasons. Raising the retry limit repeats an attempt whose inputs have not changed. Declaring the field mandatory pushes the model toward fabrication. An invented tax ID with valid syntax passes the schema and silently corrupts downstream systems. This is the hallucination risk that Anthropic warns about in Reduce hallucinations, where the recommended behavior is to let the model report that it does not have enough information. Few-shot examples are the right tool when extraction is inconsistent across document layouts. But they demonstrate judgment about content that is present, not content that is missing.

An extraction architect should classify every validation failure before deciding how to respond. Syntax errors are best prevented up front with schema-constrained structured outputs or strict tool use, as described in Structured outputs. Format and placement errors respond well to retry with feedback. Semantic inconsistencies, such as totals that do not add up, can be rechecked by the model. Absent information needs a completely different data path. Making truly optional fields nullable keeps the model honest when a value is really unavailable. Fields that downstream systems require should be sent to enrichment or human review, not left in a retry loop that can never succeed.

QUESTION: A coordinator hands each 50-document batch to an extraction subagent. When the document fetch tool times out on one file, the subagent drops its finished extractions and returns only "batch failed", so the coordinator re-runs the entire batch. What change best addresses this?
answers: Have the subagent keep retrying the fetch until the document store responds so the coordinator never sees transient errors.
Have the subagent skip the unreachable file and report the batch as fully successful so that downstream processing is never interrupted by one document.
Have the subagent retry the timed-out fetch with backoff, then return finished extractions plus structured context for any file still failing.
Move all retry decisions to the coordinator by having the subagent return "batch failed" immediately on any tool error.
feedbacks: Unlimited retries inside a subagent waste time and tokens. An outage of the document store can leave the subagent stuck for an unlimited time, while the rest of the batch is finished but not reported. Local recovery should have a limit. After that, the subagent should report what it could not resolve to the coordinator.

This is silent suppression: a failure is presented as a successful result. The coordinator and downstream systems believe every document was extracted, when one was never processed. Nobody would notice the missing record until someone downstream finds the gap. That is worse than an honest partial result.

A timeout is a transient failure. The subagent can usually resolve it by itself with one or two retries with backoff, and this keeps routine recovery away from the coordinator. If the file still cannot be fetched, the subagent returns the completed extractions together with the failed document, what was attempted, and the failure type. The coordinator can then retry only that file, or continue with the gaps marked, instead of re-running the whole batch.

This keeps the generic status, which hides which file failed and why. It also pushes routine transient handling up to the coordinator, which is the layer least able to retry a single fetch. The subagent would still throw away its completed work, so the coordinator would still have to re-run the whole batch.
prompt.explanation:
In a system with a coordinator and subagents, handle each failure at the lowest layer that can actually fix it. A timeout when fetching a document is a classic transient error. The right first response is a retry with backoff and a limit, inside the subagent. The subagent already holds the file reference, the batch state, and the extractions it has completed. This recovery does not need the coordinator's wider view. So involving the coordinator for every timeout only adds latency and noise.

When local recovery has run out of attempts, the subagent should report the problem, not hide it. Its report should contain the completed extractions, the identity of the document that could not be fetched, what was attempted, and the failure type. A structured error with partial results turns the coordinator's decision from "re-run everything" into a precise choice. It can retry one file later, send it to a different fetch path, or continue and mark the gap for downstream consumers. A plain "batch failed" status gives the coordinator none of that. This is why it re-runs 50 documents to recover one.

This design matters because Claude Agent SDK subagents run in isolated contexts. The parent only ever sees the subagent's final message, not the intermediate tool results. If the final message leaves out the finished extractions, that work is lost from the parent's point of view. The platform does return partial text when an API error stops a foreground subagent. It also provides hooks such as PostToolUseFailure for observing tool failures. But it does not automatically retry a timeout at the tool level for you. The architect must build local recovery and a well-structured final report into the subagent's instructions and tool handling.

Each of the other approaches breaks one of these principles. Marking the batch fully successful after skipping a file is silent suppression. It turns a recoverable failure into a gap in the data that nobody detects. Retrying until the store responds removes the limit on local recovery and can make the batch hang during an outage. Returning "batch failed" immediately keeps the generic status, throws away completed work, and moves transient handling to the layer with the least context. QUESTION: The pipeline's review step reports that one handler function accepts an empty email string, and a failing unit test points to the exact line. A developer asks Claude Code to add the missing check. How should this change be carried out?
answers: Enter plan mode first so Claude maps every caller of the handler before proposing the single check.
Delegate the work to an Explore subagent so the discovery output stays out of the main context.
Fork the session into two branches to compare alternative validation approaches before committing.
Run it as a direct execution request that names the file, the function, and the failing test.
feedbacks: Plan mode justifies its extra cost when the approach is uncertain, many files are involved, or the code is unfamiliar. None of those apply in this case. So a cycle of research and then approval adds formal steps to a change whose scope and location are already known.

The Explore subagent exists to isolate long output from discovery work with several phases, which would otherwise fill up the main context window. This task has no discovery phase. The failing test already identifies the line, so there is no long output to isolate.

Forking a session is useful when a shared investigation baseline should split into truly different strategies that are useful to compare. Rejecting an empty string in one function has one obvious implementation. So comparing branches spends effort on a decision that does not exist.

A single validation check in one function, located by a failing test, is a clear and small change. Its location is known, and its implementation is obvious. Direct execution with a well-scoped prompt gets the fix done without the extra cost of a planning phase that would not change the result.
prompt.explanation:
Choosing between plan mode and direct execution is a judgment of cost and benefit. It is not a safety step to perform every time. In plan mode, Claude reads files and explores the codebase without editing source. It then gives you a proposal to approve before any implementation begins. That read-only research phase is useful in three cases: when you are unsure which approach to take, when the change will touch many files, or when you do not know the code well enough to predict how far the change could reach. When none of those conditions apply, it is only extra cost.

In this situation, the pipeline itself has already resolved every uncertainty. The review step identified the problem, the failing test identified the line, and the fix is a single validation check in one function. Local bug fixes like this are a core everyday use of Claude Code. The Claude Code best practices stress that the quality of a direct request depends on how specific it is. Name the file, the function, and the test that must pass, instead of giving a vague instruction. Direct execution is reliable in this case not because it is faster, but because the prompt is well scoped. That precision gives Claude the same targeting that a plan would have produced, without a second exchange for research and approval.

Each of the other approaches solves a problem that this task does not have. Plan mode's step of mapping every caller is the right move for a refactor with architectural consequences. There, researching and proposing before any edit protects against solving the wrong problem. It adds nothing to a local guard clause. Subagents such as Explore keep large amounts of noisy research output out of the main conversation during long work with several phases. But a task with no discovery phase produces nothing that needs isolating. A subagent starts fresh, so it only adds latency to a small targeted edit. Forking a session lets two strategies develop separately from a shared analysis baseline. That matters when there are different designs that are both possible to compare. A single obvious validation does not present that choice.

One practical note for a team focused on CI: direct execution still runs under the permission mode that the session starts in. In an interactive session, the default mode asks before edits, while acceptEdits lets file edits go ahead without asking. In a non-interactive claude -p run, edits that need approval are denied unless an allow rule or an equivalent setting permits them. Choosing direct execution decides that no planning step is needed. The permission mode decides whether the resulting edits need a human to approve them.

Use direct execution with detailed instructions given in advance that spell out the intended file structure.
Run the restructuring unattended with "claude -p" so the pipeline applies it without review.
Run direct execution incrementally and switch to plan mode if complexity appears.

Every sign in the situation (many files, several workable designs, unfamiliar code) matches the documented case where planning first is worth the extra step.

Writing detailed instructions up front assumes that the developer already knows the right design and the structure of the code. The situation says this is not the case. Direct execution suits changes whose diff can be described in a sentence. It does not suit a restructuring across many files with open design choices.

The print flag is the right way to run Claude Code non-interactively for automated review and test generation. But it does not replace design review on a large architectural change. An unattended run would commit to one of several workable designs, with no chance to evaluate the plan before the edits are made.

This approach only reacts after a problem appears. By the time the complexity shows up, edits have already been made across files, and they may need to be redone. The documented workflow is to explore and plan first, then implement. It is not to plan only after direct execution runs into trouble.
prompt.explanation:
Plan mode is a permission mode in Claude Code. It is not a different model or a prompting trick. In plan mode, Claude reads files and runs exploratory commands to understand the codebase, and then writes an implementation plan. It does not edit source files until the plan is approved. Approving the plan takes the session out of plan mode, so implementation can begin. You can even open and edit the proposed plan directly before Claude continues. The mode exists to separate understanding and design from changing files. This way, expensive edits across many files happen only after the approach has been reviewed.

The decision depends on the shape of the task, not on a general preference. Anthropic's guidance is that planning is most useful in three cases: the approach is uncertain, the change touches multiple files, or the developer does not know the code well. If the diff can be described in a single sentence (a typo, a log line, a rename), plan mode adds overhead, and direct execution is preferred. This situation meets all three conditions for planning at once. There are dozens of files, several workable designs for how findings should flow into PR comments, and a developer who does not yet know that part of the code. This is the clearest example of the explore, plan, implement, commit workflow.

Each of the other approaches misjudges the task. Detailed upfront instructions assume that the design is already decided, and it is not. Starting directly and planning later leaves partly finished edits across many files, and these may contradict the design that is finally chosen. Running the change unattended with claude -p mixes up two different concerns. The print flag is correct for the team's automated review and test-generation jobs. But an architectural restructuring with open design questions needs a human to evaluate the plan before anything is written to disk.

QUESTION: This team's review service calls the Messages API with a "fetch_file" tool so Claude can request imports and tests mid-review. After the service retrieves a requested file, how must it deliver the contents so Claude can continue the analysis?
answers: Embed the fetched file contents in the "fetch_file" tool's description so Claude reads it on its next evaluation pass.
Append a user message containing a "tool_result" block whose "tool_use_id" matches the request, then resend the full history.
Send the fetched file contents as a plain user text message in a new request, since the API keeps earlier turns server-side.
Add a message with a dedicated "tool" role carrying the file contents so the API routes it to the pending request.
feedbacks: A tool definition describes what a tool does and what input it accepts. It is static metadata, not a way to pass data at runtime. Putting results into the description would make every later request larger. It would also not meet the API's requirement that each tool_use receives a matching tool_result.

The Messages API is stateless, and Claude never runs client tools itself. So the only way the model sees a result is for the application to add it to the conversation and send the whole history back. The result is sent as a tool_result block inside a user message. The block is identified by the tool_use_id from the assistant's tool_use block, and the message is placed immediately after that assistant message.

The Messages API does not keep conversation state between requests. Every call must carry the full relevant history. A plain text message with no tool_result block also leaves the pending tool_use without an answer, and the API rejects that as malformed.

Anthropic's API has only the user and assistant roles. There is no separate tool or function role. Tool results are expressed as tool_result content blocks inside an ordinary user message. They are matched to the request by tool_use_id, not by role.
prompt.explanation:
Everything about client-side tool use follows from one fact: the Messages API is stateless. Claude has no memory between requests, and it cannot run your code. When the review service offers a fetch_file tool, Claude can only ask for a file. It does this by outputting a tool_use block (with an id, the tool name, and JSON input) and stopping with stop_reason: "tool_use". From that moment, it is the harness's job to act.

The harness executes the fetch. It then builds the next request. It takes the existing messages and appends the assistant message that contained the tool_use block. Then it appends a user message whose content holds a tool_result block. This block has a tool_use_id equal to the request's id, and the file contents as its content. The result message must come immediately after the assistant's tool-use message. If the assistant requested several files in one turn, every tool_result must be returned together in that single user message, before any text block. Only when the whole history is sent again does Claude see the file and reason about the next step. That step might be requesting another file or writing its review findings. The loop repeats until stop_reason is end_turn.

The conversation history is the agent's working memory, and the application is responsible for writing it. This is why the other approaches fail. Sending a new text message assumes server-side state that does not exist. It also leaves a tool_use with no matching result, and the API rejects that. A dedicated tool role is a pattern from other providers' APIs. Anthropic deliberately keeps results inside ordinary user messages, so that the transcript stays a strict alternation of user and assistant turns. Tool descriptions are static schema metadata that Claude reads when it selects a tool. They are not a way to carry runtime data, and anything placed there would be repeated on every later call. Note also that tool results count toward the context budget. This is one reason review harnesses often trim fetched files to the relevant parts before appending them.

For teams using the SDK's Tool Runner, this cycle of appending and continuing is automated. But the underlying message format sent to the API is the same. If you edit the runner's message history yourself, you become responsible again for appending both the assistant message and the result. See Handle tool calls, How tool use works, and Working with messages.

The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.

QUESTION: This team's review prompt spells out the required finding format in detail, yet findings still alternate between concrete fixes and vague notes. Which TWO changes best restore consistent, actionable output? (Select TWO.)
answers: Have the model attach a self-rated confidence score to each finding and discard anything below a fixed threshold.
Add two to four examples that show the exact finding layout: file location, issue, severity, and a concrete fix.
Rewrite the format instructions in capital letters with phrases like ALWAYS and NEVER to raise their priority over other guidance.
Use real cases from the codebase as examples, including ambiguous ones, and show the reasoning behind each verdict.
feedbacks: Self-rated confidence is a triage signal for deciding which findings to investigate. It does not control how each finding is written. Filtering on it would hide some findings, and the remaining findings would be formatted just as inconsistently.

A small set of examples that show the exact output layout gives the model a concrete pattern to copy, instead of a description to interpret. This is the documented next step when detailed instructions alone still let the format change from one finding to the next.

Emphasis only changes the relative priority of an instruction. The model is already reading that instruction and interpreting it inconsistently. The instructions in this situation are already detailed, so stronger wording adds no practical information. It does not close the gap between describing the format and demonstrating it.

Examples work best when they closely match the real use case and cover the edge cases where the model is inconsistent. Showing the reasoning next to each verdict teaches the judgment behind the format. The model then applies that judgment to new findings, instead of only copying the samples.
prompt.explanation:
This situation is the classic point where few-shot examples are justified. The instructions are already clear and specific, but the output still varies from run to run. Anthropic's guidance on increasing consistency states clearly that showing examples of the desired output constrains format better than abstract instructions do. The reason is mechanical. A written description of a format still has to be interpreted, and every interpretation is a chance for the format to change. A worked example removes that interpretation step, because it gives the model a concrete artifact to match. For a CI reviewer, this means two to four findings written in the form the pipeline wants. Each has a location, an issue statement, a severity, and a concrete fix.

Which examples you choose matters as much as whether you include them. The documented properties of good examples are these. They are relevant: they match the real inputs the model will see. They are diverse: they cover the edge cases without introducing unintended patterns. They are structured: each is wrapped in an XML tag named example, or several are placed inside a tag named examples, so the model can tell demonstration apart from instruction. Take examples from real code in the repository, including the ambiguous cases where the reviewer is currently inconsistent. Add the reasoning for each verdict. This lets the model learn the judgment, not only repeat the sample text. A small, targeted set is better than a large one. Too many examples dilute attention and push out the instructions they are meant to support.

The other two approaches fix different problems, or no problem at all. Writing the same instruction in capitals with ALWAYS and NEVER only changes the priority order among rules that the model already fails to apply uniformly. Emphasis should be used for only a few critical constraints, and it does not replace a demonstration. Self-rated confidence scores are useful for directing human attention toward uncertain findings. But they do nothing to change how a finding is written. Discarding low-confidence items only removes output; it does not make the remaining output consistent.

Keep one limit in mind: examples shape format and judgment, but they are not a hard guarantee of structure that a machine can parse. When the pipeline must parse JSON byte for byte, the stronger mechanisms are Structured outputs via output_config.format with a JSON schema, or a tool definition whose input schema is the finding format. Those enforce syntax and shape. Few-shot examples are what make the content inside that shape consistently actionable. See Increase output consistency, Claude prompting best practices, and Structured outputs.

QUESTION: The structured review findings this team emits use a "category" enum limited to "bug", "security", "performance", and "style". Licensing and accessibility findings are being squeezed into "style" and routed to the wrong reviewers. Which schema change best handles findings outside the listed categories?
answers: Make the category field optional so the model can leave it empty whenever no listed value fits a finding.
Replace the enum with an unconstrained string so the model can label each finding with whatever category it sees fit.
Add an "other" value to the category enum together with a free-text field that describes the uncategorized finding.
Add a prompt instruction telling the model to choose the closest existing category whenever a finding does not fit clearly.
feedbacks: Optional or nullable fields are the right design when the source material may not contain the information. They prevent the model from inventing a value. But a review finding always has some category. So leaving the field empty throws away useful information and gives the routing step nothing to act on.

Removing the enum replaces a mislabeling problem with an inconsistency problem. The model may output "Security", "sec", and "vulnerability" for the same kind of finding. Downstream routing depends on a closed, predictable set of values, and an unconstrained string cannot provide that.

An open enum keeps every known category as a stable value that a machine can route. It also gives the model an honest option for findings that really do not fit. The paired detail string keeps the information about what the finding actually is. So the team can route it by hand, and later add kinds that appear often as full enum values.

This instruction makes the behavior that causes the misrouting into a formal rule, because the closest category for a licensing issue is still wrong. Prompt wording cannot fix a schema that offers no correct answer for some inputs. The schema itself has to provide a valid place for those findings.
prompt.explanation:
A closed enum forces a choice. When the model is limited to a fixed list of values, every finding must be assigned one of them, even when none is correct. Grammar-constrained structured output guarantees that the value will be a member of the list. But it says nothing about whether the list itself covers the inputs the system actually receives. When a review finding is about licensing or accessibility, and the only options are bug, security, performance, and style, the schema has made a wrong answer certain. The symptom (findings sent to the wrong reviewers) comes from a design problem in the schema, not from the model failing to follow instructions.

The standard fix is an open enum. Keep the known categories as enum values, add an other value, and pair it with a free-text detail field such as category_detail. The model fills in this field when it selects other. This keeps both properties the team needs. Known categories stay routable by machine, because they are still constrained scalar values. Unknown categories are not silently mislabeled or dropped, because the detail string records what the finding actually is. Over time, the detail strings also help the team discover new categories. If licensing appears again and again, it can get its own enum value. The same reasoning supports an unclear value for cases that the model cannot classify with confidence. That is more useful than a confident wrong label. Anthropic's structured outputs documentation notes that enums must use scalar values. It also notes that enum capitalization is not fully guaranteed, so applications should compare enum values without regard to case. This convention is built on those documented features.

It helps to keep two schema design choices separate. Required versus optional answers the question "might the source not contain this?" Marking a field optional or nullable prevents the model from inventing a value to fill a required field. Open versus closed enums answers a different question: "might a real value exist that is not on my list?" Making category optional applies the first choice to the second problem. Every finding has a category, so an empty value loses information instead of preventing fabrication. Replacing the enum with a free string goes too far in the other direction, and it gives up the consistency that routing depends on. Instructing the model to pick the nearest category only turns the mislabeling into a rule. Schema design should give the model a truthful option for every input it may receive. See Structured outputs and Define tools for the supported schema features and guidance on required and optional parameters.

QUESTION: A developer on this team wants to experiment with a stricter version of the shared /pr-review skill in local sessions, running it side by side with the team's version for comparison, without changing what teammates or the pipeline see. How should the variant be set up?
answers: Commit the stricter variant as "pr-review-strict" in the repository's .claude/skills/ directory.
Add the stricter review rules to the developer's ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md so they apply in every local session.
Create the stricter variant in ~/.claude/skills/ under a different name such as "pr-review-strict".
Create the stricter variant in ~/.claude/skills/pr-review/ so it loads only in the developer's own sessions.
feedbacks: Anything committed under the repository's .claude/skills/ is shared with every teammate on their next pull, and it then appears in their skill menu. That changes what the team sees, which is the outcome the developer wants to avoid while experimenting.

Content in the user-level CLAUDE.md is always loaded into every session instead of being invoked on demand. So it is not a separate skill that the developer can choose to run or not run. It would also be applied during the shared /pr-review runs, which makes a fair comparison between the two versions impossible.

Personal skills under ~/.claude/skills/ stay on the developer's machine and are never shared through version control, so teammates and the pipeline are not affected. Giving the variant its own name keeps the shared /pr-review skill available to invoke next to it. A side-by-side comparison needs both skills to be available in the same session.

This does keep the variant out of the repository. However, a personal skill takes precedence over a project skill with the same name. The developer would then lose access to the team's version in local sessions, so the two versions could not be run side by side.
prompt.explanation:
Claude Code loads skills from several locations, and the location decides who gets them. A project skill at .claude/skills/NAME/SKILL.md is part of the repository. Committing it gives it to every teammate and to any pipeline that checks out the code. A personal skill at ~/.claude/skills/NAME/SKILL.md exists only on one machine, and it loads in all of that user's projects on that machine. The repository is shared with the team, and the home directory belongs to one person. An experiment that should not reach other people belongs in the home directory.

Location is not the only factor, because skills also take precedence by name. When a personal skill and a project skill have the same name, the personal one wins, and the project one is hidden in that user's sessions. A personal copy with the same name is useful when you want to replace the shared behavior for yourself on purpose. In this question it defeats the goal, because the developer wants to call both versions in the same session and compare their findings. Giving the variant a different name, such as pr-review-strict, keeps the shared /pr-review unchanged and adds the experimental skill next to it. Note that the frontmatter (the settings block at the top of the file) name field can also set the invocation name, so the variant must not declare the shared name there by accident.

Each of the other approaches breaks one of the two requirements. Committing the variant into .claude/skills/ shares it with the team immediately. That is the right step only after the experiment has been shown to work and the team should adopt it. Putting the stricter rules into ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md turns an on-demand workflow into guidance that is always loaded. It cannot be invoked selectively, and it would also change the output of the shared skill. This is why CLAUDE.md is used for conventions that always apply, not for task-specific procedures. Once the variant is under ~/.claude/skills/, Claude Code picks up changes to it during a running session, so the developer can keep adjusting the stricter review criteria without restarting.

See Claude Code skills for personal versus project skill locations and name precedence, and Claude Code features overview for how skills, CLAUDE.md, and other configuration surfaces differ.

QUESTION: A developer reports that this team's review prompt produces far fewer style findings in their local Claude Code session than when the CI job runs the identical prompt against the same repository checkout. What is the best first diagnostic step?
answers: Run /context in the developer's local session and check the Memory files list against what CI loads.
Re-run the CI job several times and keep the run whose findings match the developer's local results.
Run "claude doctor" on the CI runner to list any settings entries that were rejected when the job started.
Add stronger wording to the project CLAUDE.md instructing Claude to ignore style issues during review.
feedbacks: The /context command lists the memory files that a session has loaded, in its Memory files section. This is the fastest way to find personal instruction files that change local behavior. User-level instructions in the home directory and uncommitted local files never reach a CI runner. So comparing what the local session loaded against the committed project files identifies the source of the difference.

Retrying and picking the run you like assumes the difference is random variation. A consistent gap between two environments on the same checkout points to a configuration difference instead. Choosing a favorable run leaves the cause in place, and the next pull request will show the same inconsistency.

Settings diagnostics such as /status and claude doctor report which settings sources loaded or which settings entries were rejected. Settings control permissions, hooks, and similar behavior. They do not hold the persistent review instructions that Claude follows. A difference in how strictly style issues are flagged points to a difference in loaded instructions, and settings diagnostics do not show that.

Stronger prompt wording treats the symptom without knowing the cause, and it may move the CI output away from what the team wants. The developer's local session already produces the desired result. So the task is to find what that session loads differently, not to guess at new instructions.
prompt.explanation:
Claude Code builds its instructions from a hierarchy of memory files. The first thing to understand about this hierarchy is which files are part of the repository and which are not. User-level instructions in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md apply to one person on one machine. CLAUDE.local.md is also personal and is usually kept out of version control. Committed project memory files are what a teammate, or a CI runner that clones the repository, actually receives. These are ./CLAUDE.md or ./.claude/CLAUDE.md, together with any committed directory-level CLAUDE.md files that apply to the working directory. User-level and uncommitted local memory files are not part of the checkout. All of these files are concatenated into context instead of overriding each other. So a developer's personal file adds guidance on top of the shared project guidance in every local session, and nothing makes this visible.

This design is deliberate. Personal preferences should not leak into the team's shared configuration, and shared conventions should not depend on any one person's home directory. The cost is the situation in this question: two environments run the same prompt on the same checkout and behave differently, because one of them loads an extra file. Do not guess. The right first step is to make the loaded set of files visible. Running /context in the local session shows the memory files that Claude Code loaded, under Memory files. Comparing that list against the committed project files tells you immediately whether personal instructions, for example a rule to skip small style issues, are changing the local output.

The other approaches look at the wrong layer. /status reports which settings sources loaded, and claude doctor lists rejected settings entries. But settings files control permissions, hooks, environment, and model selection. They do not hold persistent review instructions, so they cannot explain a difference in what gets flagged. Rewriting the project CLAUDE.md with firmer language before diagnosing the gap is prompt tuning without information. It also ignores the fact that the local configuration already produces the intended behavior. After the personal file is identified, its relevant content can be moved into the project CLAUDE.md so that CI and every teammate get it. Re-running CI and keeping a matching run mistakes a stable configuration difference for nondeterminism, and the next pipeline run will be just as inconsistent.

See Manage Claude's memory for the file locations, load order, and the /context check, and Claude Code settings for what settings files and settings diagnostics do and do not control.

QUESTION: This team's pipeline step launches the "claude" command with the review prompt as an argument, but every job waits with no activity until the runner's timeout kills it and no review is ever produced. What change fixes the step?
answers: Set "--permission-mode acceptEdits" so the run never pauses waiting for approval of file edits.
Run the command with the "-p" flag so it processes the prompt, prints the result, and exits.
Add "--output-format json" so the result is emitted as machine-readable output the pipeline can parse.
Raise the pipeline step's timeout so the review has enough time to finish before the runner kills it.
feedbacks: Permission modes control which tool actions proceed without approval. That matters only after a run is already non-interactive. The step in the scenario never gets that far, because it opens an interactive session. Changing the permission baseline does not change the session type, so the job still waits for terminal input.

Without the print flag, the CLI starts an interactive session that waits for terminal input, and that input never arrives on a CI runner. The "-p" (or "--print") flag is the documented way to run Claude Code non-interactively. It processes the prompt, writes the result to standard output, and exits with a status code that the pipeline can act on.

The "--output-format" option controls how print-mode results are formatted. It is useful once results are being produced, for example to post structured findings as PR comments. It applies to print mode, but it does not put the CLI into non-interactive mode by itself, so the job still hangs.

The job is not slow. It is waiting for interactive input that will never come. A longer timeout only delays the failure and wastes runner minutes, because an interactive session never finishes on its own in an unattended environment.
prompt.explanation:
Claude Code has two very different ways of running. When it is launched without flags, it opens an interactive terminal session that keeps reading from the keyboard until the user ends it. When it is launched with -p (long form --print), it runs in non-interactive mode. It takes the prompt, runs the agent loop (including any tool calls it is permitted to make), writes the final result to standard output, and exits. A CI runner has no person at a terminal, so an interactive session just waits. That is why a job that uses the plain command stays idle until the timeout kills it, and why -p is the flag that makes the step usable in a pipeline.

Think of claude -p as the command-line form of the Claude Agent SDK. Anthropic documents it as the way to run the agent loop from scripts and CI/CD when you do not want to write Python or TypeScript, and programs in other languages can run it as a subprocess. Because it is built for automation, the related behaviors are designed for pipelines too. The process exits with code 0 on success and non-zero on failure, so a pipeline step can pass or fail based on it. Piped standard input is supported, so you can feed file contents into the prompt. --output-format json (optionally with --json-schema) returns the result in a structure that a script can parse, for example to post inline PR comments. These output options add to print mode. They do not replace it, which is why adding a JSON format alone does not stop the hang.

Permission settings are the other thing an unattended run needs, but they solve a different problem. Once a run is non-interactive, flags such as --allowedTools or --permission-mode decide which tool actions proceed without a person approving them. This prevents the agent from stopping at a prompt that nobody will answer. Setting a permission mode on a session that is still interactive does not change the session type. In the same way, raising the step timeout treats a blocking wait as if it were slowness. The review would never finish, no matter how long the runner waited.

Once the step runs with -p, the remaining pipeline design choices follow the same automation approach. Give the run project context through CLAUDE.md (review criteria, testing standards, fixture conventions). Use an independent instance for review instead of the session that wrote the code. Consider --bare for scripted calls when you want to skip auto-discovery of hooks, plugins, and MCP servers so that startup is faster. See Run Claude Code programmatically and the CLI reference for the full set of print-mode options.

QUESTION: The review agent in this pipeline reads CI results from three MCP servers, two of them third-party, that return mixed formats: Unix timestamps, ISO 8601 dates, and numeric build states. It sometimes misreports a failed build as passing in PR comments. What is the most maintainable fix?
answers: Expose a custom "normalize_result" MCP tool and instruct the agent to call it after every CI data fetch.
Document each server's timestamp and build state conventions in the project CLAUDE.md so the agent interprets them.
Register a "PostToolUse" hook matched to those tools that rewrites each result into one consistent format.
Build proxy MCP servers around the third-party ones that reformat their responses before returning them.
feedbacks: This makes normalization an extra step that the model must remember to take. That is probabilistic, not guaranteed. The raw, misleading output also enters the context before any normalization happens. It adds a round trip to every fetch and a custom tool to maintain, when a hook already covers the need.

CLAUDE.md is guidance that the model usually follows, but it is not an enforced transformation. A numeric state code can still be misread on any run. Reading mixed formats correctly in every PR comment needs a deterministic step in code, not more instructions that compete for the model's attention.

A PostToolUse hook runs after a tool returns, and it can replace the tool output before the model sees it. So every result arrives in one normalized format, no matter which server produced it. The transformation is in code at a single interception point. It works for third-party servers that the team cannot change, and it does not depend on the model remembering a convention.

Wrapping each external server in its own proxy repeats the normalization logic in several components, and it must be done again for every new source. A hook gets the same result at one point in the agent loop, with much less to maintain.
prompt.explanation:
In the Claude Code and Agent SDK loop, a tool call does not go to the model directly. The harness runs the tool and then adds the result to the conversation. Hooks are the documented interception points around this exchange. A PostToolUse hook fires after a tool has run successfully. It receives the tool name, the input that was used, and the tool response. Its output can either add additionalContext next to the result or supply updatedToolOutput, which replaces what Claude sees. Data normalization needs this replacement ability. Unix timestamps become ISO 8601 strings, numeric build states become words like "failed" or "passed", and the model only ever reasons over one consistent format. For MCP tools, the hook matcher uses the mcp__SERVER__ACTION naming pattern. So the same hook can be limited to the three CI servers without affecting other tools.

The important distinction is between deterministic enforcement and probabilistic guidance. CLAUDE.md conventions, system prompt notes, and an instruction to call a normalization tool all depend on the model applying them on each run. A review that sometimes reports a failed build as passing is the kind of error that makes people stop trusting automated feedback. A hook runs as code on every matching call, whether or not the model thinks about it. It does this no matter who owns the server, which is why it is better than building proxy servers around third-party sources.

Two limits matter when you design this. First, a PostToolUse hook changes only what the model sees after the tool has already run. It cannot prevent or change the call itself; that is the job of PreToolUse. Second, for built-in tools the replacement output must match the tool's output format, but MCP tool output is passed through without schema validation, so normalizing MCP results is straightforward. Note also that returning a decision of block from PostToolUse does not hide the original output. It only attaches a reason, so rewriting results requires updatedToolOutput. See Agent SDK hooks and the Claude Code hooks reference.

QUESTION: The review step in this pipeline emits findings as JSON, and a validator rejects roughly one run in ten because a finding's "line" value falls outside the pull request diff. The team wants the step to recover automatically on the next attempt. What should the retry request contain?
answers: Include the original diff plus a general note that the previous attempt was invalid and must be regenerated.
Resubmit the same prompt unchanged, relying on a fresh sample to land every line inside the diff.
Include the original diff, the rejected output, and the exact validation error identifying the out-of-range finding.
Resend the original prompt with stronger wording insisting that every cited line number must fall inside the diff.
feedbacks: Telling the model only that something was wrong does not tell it which finding or which field to fix. Without the specific error, the retry is hardly better than a fresh sample. It may repeat the same out-of-range line or break something else.

Sending the identical request again treats the failure as random noise instead of a mistake that can be corrected. Retries with no new information waste a full review run each time. The failure rate on the second attempt stays about the same as on the first.

This is the retry-with-error-feedback pattern. The model sees what it was given, what it produced, and what was wrong, so it can correct the specific finding instead of guessing. An out-of-range line is an application-level semantic validation failure. But the model can re-check it against the diff it has, and this pattern usually fixes this kind of error in one or two attempts.

Stronger wording changes nothing about the specific output that failed. The model already received a prompt that asked for findings tied to the diff. Emphasis without the specific error still leaves the model to find the mistake on its own. That is the weaker approach when the validator already knows what went wrong.
prompt.explanation:
Schema enforcement and content validation solve different problems. When the pipeline runs with a JSON schema, the format of the response is handled for you. Examples are --output-format json together with --json-schema in Claude Code, or Structured outputs on the Messages API. Fields are present, types are correct, and no retry is needed for schema violations. A normal fixed output schema does not by itself check whether a line number is actually in the diff, whether a severity matches the rubric, or whether a cited fix exists. Those are semantic, application-level checks. Unless you build them into a custom validator, they belong in your own validation code.

When that validator rejects a run, the documented way to recover is the validation-retry loop. Send Claude the original input, the previous (incorrect) output, and the specific error. An example error is "finding 3 cites src/billing/invoice.ts:212, but the diff for that file only covers lines 40 to 95." The model now has an instruction it can act on, and it can re-check its work instead of starting again from nothing. One or two such retries usually fix format, structural, and content errors that the model can check against the material it was given. The same principle applies in tool use. An invalid call is answered with a tool_result marked is_error: true and a precise message, such as the name of a missing parameter, and Claude retries with corrected input a limited number of times. The specific error text is what turns a retry into a correction.

It also helps to know when this loop will not help. Retries fix errors that the model can repair from the material it has: a wrong format, a field in the wrong place, an arithmetic inconsistency, a line outside the diff. They do nothing when the needed information is missing from the input, for example when the finding depends on a file that was never provided. Limit the loop to one or two attempts, and send persistent failures to a human instead of looping forever. This application-level loop is also separate from the SDK's automatic HTTP retries for timeouts and 5xx responses. Those retry the transport, not the content.

Each of the other approaches misses how this works. Sending the same prompt again depends on sampling luck and gives the model no new information. A general "that was invalid" note tells the model that something failed but not what, so it must find the problem itself. Stronger wording in the original prompt is the common trap of making an instruction the model already had more emphatic. It adds emphasis but does not give the one fact that the validator already knows. See Structured outputs for what schemas do and do not guarantee, and Handle tool calls for the documented pattern of returning specific errors so Claude can correct its next attempt.
