SCENARIO: You are integrating Claude Code into your Continuous Integration/Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.

QUESTION: The pipeline's test generator receives the existing tests for each changed file. When those tests cover only one branch of a conditional, the generator is inconsistent: sometimes it proposes a test for the other branch, and sometimes it says the function is already covered. Detailed coverage instructions have not helped. What addition most reliably fixes this inconsistency?
answers: Include the project's entire test suite in the prompt so the model has complete coverage context.
Run the generator three times per changed file and keep only tests proposed in at least two runs.
Add two or three examples of partly tested functions that show whether to test the other branch and why.
Add an explicit rule stating that every untested conditional branch must always receive a new test.
feedbacks: The generator already sees the tests that matter for the changed file. What is missing is not information but a consistent judgment about what counts as a coverage gap. Filling the prompt with unrelated tests spreads the model's attention over more material, and it does nothing to make the decision consistent.

Majority voting over a judgment that has no clear basis only averages the inconsistency. It can remove a correct branch test that appeared in a single run as easily as it filters out noise. It also triples the cost, and it never teaches the model how to make the decision.

Few-shot examples show a partly tested function, its existing test, and the reasoning for proposing or skipping a branch test. This gives the model a concrete decision boundary that it can generalize from. This is the kind of ambiguous case where examples work better than written instructions, because they demonstrate the judgment instead of restating a rule.

The question states that detailed coverage instructions have already failed to make the behavior consistent. Adding one more rule tries to solve the same problem with the same tool. The hard part is recognizing when a branch is really uncovered and when it is already exercised by another test by chance. Written rules communicate that kind of judgment poorly.
prompt.explanation:
Test generation for partly covered functions is a typical ambiguous-case problem. A rule like "write tests for untested branches" sounds clear, but the model still has to make judgments. It must decide whether an existing test that passes through an if by chance counts as coverage. It must decide whether a trivial else that only returns a default needs a test. It must tell a real gap from one that is already handled elsewhere. When detailed instructions produce behavior that changes between runs, the instructions are not failing because they lack emphasis. They fail because they describe the goal without demonstrating the decision.

This is where few-shot examples are most useful. Anthropic describes well-chosen examples as one of the most reliable ways to control output format, structure, and consistency. The guidance stresses that examples should be relevant, and varied enough to cover edge cases. Use two or three examples that each show a partly tested function, its existing test, and the decision with its reasoning. For example: "the existing test only reaches the early return, so the validation branch still needs a case" versus "both branches are exercised through the parametrized test, so no new test is proposed". Examples like these let the model apply the same boundary to functions it has never seen. The reasoning matters as much as the verdict. Examples that show why one action is better than a plausible alternative teach judgment, not just format. Wrap the examples in a clearly marked block so Claude can tell them apart from instructions. Examples add to explicit criteria; they do not replace them.

Each of the other approaches misses the root cause. Restating the rule more forcefully repeats a technique that has already proven insufficient in this case. Adding the whole test suite to the context gives the model material it does not need for this file and spreads its attention over more text, when the relevant tests are already present. Majority voting across repeated runs reduces run-to-run noise statistically, but the judgment itself still has no clear basis. So the consensus is still a vote over an inconsistent decision rule, and it discards real coverage gaps that appeared in only one run. Whatever change is made, test it with an evaluation set that deliberately includes ambiguous partial-coverage cases, because those are the inputs where behavior changes from run to run.

See Claude prompting best practices for guidance on multishot examples and ambiguous-case prompting, and Develop tests for building evaluations that cover edge cases.

The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.

QUESTION: When a changed function depends on a helper defined in another file, the automated reviewer behaves inconsistently: it flags a bug without reading the helper, reads the helper and still flags correct code, or skips the case entirely. Prose rules describing when to read, flag, or skip have not fixed this. What addition is most effective?
answers: Add an emphatic rule that the reviewer must read every imported file before reporting any finding on a pull request.
Ask the reviewer to rate its confidence on each cross-file finding and drop any finding below a fixed threshold.
Add two to four examples of ambiguous cross-file cases, each showing the action taken and why it beat the alternatives.
Add twenty or more examples covering every import pattern in the codebase so no cross-file case is left unaddressed.
feedbacks: This is a stronger version of the prose (ordinary sentences, not structured data) instructions that have already proven insufficient. It is also too broad, because many findings have nothing to do with imports. And it does nothing about the case where the reviewer reads the helper and still flags correct code. That is a failure of judgment, not a missing read.

Self-rated confidence is poorly calibrated, and it does not change how the reviewer decides whether to read, flag, or skip. Filtering on it hides some bad findings but also removes real ones. The inconsistency itself is not fixed.

The reviewer's problem is a judgment boundary, not a missing rule, and prose (ordinary sentences, not structured data) has already failed to teach that judgment. A small set of targeted examples shows the chosen action together with a short reason for rejecting the other plausible actions. This demonstrates the decision logic, so the model can apply it to new cross-file situations.

Adding many examples makes the prompt much longer and weakens the signal from the few cases that are actually on the ambiguous boundary. Few-shot prompting works by teaching a decision rule that the model generalizes. It does not work by listing every situation the model might meet.
prompt.explanation:
The failure in this scenario is a decision boundary problem. The reviewer must choose among three plausible actions: read the helper, flag, or skip. Nothing in the prompt currently explains how to choose between them. Written instructions describe rules, but a rule like "read related files when needed" leaves "when needed" open to interpretation, and the model interprets it differently on every run. This is the situation where few-shot examples work better than more instructions. An example shows a borderline case, the action that was taken, and a short reason why that action was better than the alternatives. It demonstrates the judgment instead of describing it, and the model applies the pattern to cases it has never seen.

The examples should be few and targeted. Use two to four cases that are on the ambiguous boundary. For instance: a helper whose return type is not obvious from the call site, a well-known helper that does not need to be read, and a case where reading the helper shows that the flagged code is correct. These teach the distinction efficiently. Anthropic's guidance is that examples should be relevant to the real use case and varied enough to cover edge cases without teaching unintended patterns. They should also be clearly separated from the rest of the prompt by wrapping each one in an XML tag named example, with the group wrapped in a tag named examples. Keep any reasoning in the examples short: one sentence of evidence or explanation, not a demand for step-by-step internal reasoning in the output.

The other approaches fall short for different reasons. An emphatic "always read every import" rule is more of the same prose (ordinary sentences, not structured data) that has already failed. It also does not address the case where the reviewer reads the helper and still flags correct code, because that failure is about judging what was read, not about reading it. Twenty or more examples turn a focused demonstration into noise. The value of few-shot prompting comes from well-targeted examples, not from covering every pattern. Confidence-threshold filtering depends on self-reported scores that are poorly calibrated, and it throws away findings instead of improving the decision that produces them.

See Claude prompting best practices and Increase output consistency for guidance on constraining behavior with well-chosen examples.

SCENARIO: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.

QUESTION: The document analysis subagent keeps running built-in Grep over downloaded files instead of calling its MCP tool "search_corpus". That tool returns ranked passages with source citations and page numbers, but its description says only "Searches research documents." Which TWO changes most directly fix this preference? (Select TWO.)
answers: Add a rule to the subagent's system prompt stating it must always call search_corpus instead of Grep for every lookup.
Add text to the tool's description saying when to use it instead of plain text search over the files.
Rename the tool to grep_corpus so the agent associates it with the built-in search tool it already favors.
Expand the description to list the ranked passages, source citations, and page numbers it returns that Grep cannot.
feedbacks: A general prompt rule affects behavior probabilistically, and it does not explain what the tool is for. So the model still lacks the information it needs when it chooses a tool. Anthropic also warns against absolute "always use this tool" instructions. They cause over-triggering on tasks such as exact identifier lookups, where Grep is the right choice.

Good tool descriptions state when to use the tool and when not to. This draws the line between semantic retrieval and literal string matching. With that line written into the description, the model can send conceptual research queries to the MCP tool and still use Grep for exact identifiers, instead of using Grep for everything by default.

Copying the built-in tool's name makes the two tools look like they overlap, instead of making them look different. That overlap is the known cause of wrong tool choices. Tool selection depends on descriptions much more than on names. A confusing name with a one-line description does nothing to tell the model what the MCP tool does better.

The description is the main signal the model uses when it chooses between tools. A built-in tool with a familiar purpose wins by default against a one-line MCP description. Listing the concrete outputs that the MCP tool provides (ranked passages with citations and page numbers, which Grep does not produce) gives the model a reason to prefer it when that output matters.
prompt.explanation:
Claude chooses among available tools almost entirely from what their descriptions tell it. Anthropic calls a detailed description by far the most important factor in tool performance. Suppose a subagent has a built-in tool such as Grep and also an MCP tool whose description is one vague sentence. The built-in tool usually wins. The model already has a clear, well-described idea of what Grep does, while "Searches research documents" gives it no reason to believe that the MCP tool does anything different or better. The documented fix is to improve the MCP description so that it points out the unique data and context that the built-in tool cannot provide.

Two kinds of content do most of this work. First, describe the outputs. Ranked passages, source citations, and page numbers are the information that a research pipeline with many citations needs. Grep, whose default output mode returns only matching file paths, cannot supply them. Second, describe when the tool applies. State that the tool handles conceptual or topical queries across the indexed corpus, and that literal string matching over local files is still a job for Grep. Anthropic recommends at least three or four sentences that cover what a tool does, when to use it and when not to, what it returns, and what it does not return. In Claude Code with tool search enabled, MCP tool descriptions are deferred until needed, and server instructions load first. So the server's instructions should be just as clear. The most important words for tool choice should come early in the text, because long descriptions are truncated.

The other approaches miss how tool selection works. A system prompt rule to always use search_corpus leaves the description empty and depends on probabilistic compliance. It also causes over-triggering on exact identifier lookups, where Grep is appropriate. Anthropic specifically warns against general "always use this tool" prompting. Renaming the tool to look like grep creates overlap with the built-in tool, which is the usual cause of wrong tool choices, and names carry much less weight than descriptions anyway. If a competing built-in tool must really be unavailable, the correct control is tool availability on the subagent definition or a permission rule, not wording. But the scenario asks how to fix the preference while both tools remain available.

See Define tools for description best practices, Claude Code MCP for how MCP descriptions and server instructions are loaded, and Claude Code tools for what the built-in Grep actually returns.

SCENARIO: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.

QUESTION: The team's shared MCP configuration must supply the search API key and the hosted document service's bearer token to every teammate, without committing either secret to the repository. Which TWO practices achieve this? (Select TWO.)
answers: Set the document service entry's "headers" field to "Authorization: Bearer ${DOCS_API_TOKEN}" so the token expands at runtime.
Reference the search key as "${SEARCH_API_KEY}" in the stdio server's "env" field so it expands from each developer's shell.
Write the literal secrets into ".mcp.json" at the project root and add that file to ".gitignore" so the keys never reach the remote.
Put the real key as the fallback in "${SEARCH_API_KEY:-sk-live-9f3a}" so the configuration works before anyone sets a shell variable.
feedbacks: For remote HTTP servers, the "headers" field also supports environment variable expansion. So a bearer token can be referenced by name instead of being written literally. The committed configuration contains no secret, and each teammate's environment provides the token when Claude Code connects.

The "env" field of a server entry in ".mcp.json" supports "${VAR}" expansion. The committed file contains only the variable name, and each developer's environment supplies the real key at runtime. The server definition is shared through version control, and the secret is never placed in the repository.

Ignoring ".mcp.json" keeps the secrets out of the repository, but it also keeps the server definitions out. Teammates no longer receive the shared configuration when they clone or pull. This defeats the purpose of a project-scoped file, which exists to be checked in and shared.

The "${VAR:-default}" syntax is real. But putting the actual key as the default writes the secret directly into the committed file. A fallback is appropriate for values that are not sensitive, like a default URL or path. It is not appropriate for credentials.
prompt.explanation:
Claude Code separates MCP server configuration into scopes. The project scope is a .mcp.json file at the repository root. It is meant to be committed so that everyone on the team connects to the same servers. This design creates an obvious conflict, because a shared file is the one place where you must not write API keys. The solution is environment variable expansion. Inside .mcp.json, the syntax ${VAR} is replaced at runtime with the value of VAR from the developer's environment, and ${VAR:-default} supplies a fallback value when the variable is not set. Expansion works in the command, args, env, url, and headers fields. This covers both local stdio servers (credentials passed through env) and remote HTTP servers (credentials passed as an Authorization header).

The repository holds the structure of the integration: which server, how to launch or reach it, and which variable names it needs. Each machine holds the secrets. For the research system, the web search server's key goes in the stdio entry's env block as ${SEARCH_API_KEY}. The hosted document service's token goes in its headers block as Bearer ${DOCS_API_TOKEN}. Claude Code's inspection commands, such as claude mcp list and claude mcp get, show the variable reference instead of the resolved value, so the secret does not leak through tooling either. One limit to know: certain reserved credential names, such as ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, are deliberately not expanded in remote url or headers fields. So use custom variable names for third-party services.

The incorrect approaches fail in opposite directions. Adding .mcp.json to the git ignore list protects the secret but gives up the sharing benefit. Every teammate must then recreate the configuration by hand, which is the problem the project scope was created to avoid. Putting the real key in a :-default fallback does the reverse. It keeps sharing but commits the secret in plain text. The convenience of working without shell setup is the convenience you do not want for credentials. Defaults are useful for values that are not sensitive, like a base URL or a local path that differs between machines.

See Connect Claude Code to tools via MCP for scopes and expansion rules, and MCP in the Agent SDK for how the research system's query() call loads .mcp.json and passes credentials through env and headers.

QUESTION: The web search subagent's MCP search tool sets "isError" to true whenever its result list is empty, so the coordinator retries zero-match queries as if the search service were down. How should the tool report a query that legitimately matches no sources?
answers: Silently retry the search with broader terms until at least one source can be returned.
Return a JSON-RPC protocol error so the MCP host handles the condition instead of the model.
Return a normal result with "isError" false and content stating that no sources matched the query.
Return "isError" true with an "errorCategory" of transient so the coordinator knows to retry later.
feedbacks: Broadening the query automatically inside the tool changes what was actually searched, and it does not tell the coordinator. This can return irrelevant sources that look like answers to the original query. The coordinator also loses the information that the specific query matched nothing, and it needs that information to change the direction of the research.

Protocol errors are for problems such as unknown tools, invalid arguments, or server faults. The MCP client handles them, and they are not shown to the model as a tool result. An empty search result is not a protocol problem. Sending it through that channel hides the outcome from the agent that needs to act on it.

A query that runs successfully and finds nothing is a valid outcome, not a failure of the tool. Reporting it as a normal result with a clear "no matches" message lets the coordinator tell an empty answer apart from an outage. The coordinator can then decide to rewrite the query instead of retrying the same call.

Labeling a zero-match query as a transient error tells the coordinator that waiting and retrying will eventually produce results. That is false for a query that has no matches. This keeps the retry loop that the team wants to remove, and it labels a successful empty result as an access failure.
prompt.explanation:
The MCP tool result carries two different kinds of information: whether the tool ran correctly, and what it found. The isError flag answers only the first question. A search that reaches its backend, runs the query, and gets zero hits has run correctly; the empty set is its real answer. Marking that outcome as an error combines two very different situations into one signal. One is an access failure that a retry might fix. The other is a valid empty result that no retry will change. The coordinator in this system has only one interpretation of that signal, so it retries.

isError: true is meant for tool execution failures, such as upstream timeouts, invalid input data, or refusals because of business rules. In these cases the model can read the message and try to recover. A separate channel, the JSON-RPC protocol error, exists for structural problems like unknown tool names or malformed arguments. The MCP client handles those, and they never reach the model as a visible tool result. So they are the wrong place for a domain outcome like an empty search. The MCP specification describes this split between protocol errors and tool errors at MCP Tools specification, and the SDK guidance at MCP server error handling explains why errors that the model should see go in the result and not in the protocol layer.

Returning a normal result with isError false and content that clearly says no sources matched gives the coordinator an accurate picture. The search service is healthy. The query was too narrow, or few sources cover the topic. The right next step is a rewritten query, or a coverage gap noted in the report. Labeling the same outcome as a transient error causes pointless retries. Having the tool quietly broaden the search hides the true result of the original query behind sources that the coordinator never asked for. In a research system that cites its evidence, this hidden substitution is worse than an honest empty answer. On the Anthropic side, the equivalent tool_result block uses is_error, with the same principle: set it only when execution actually failed. See Handle tool calls.

SCENARIO: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.

QUESTION: Reports often have thin sections even though the first breakdown of the topic was correct: a grid-storage report covered batteries in depth but gave hydrogen only two sentences. The team wants such gaps closed automatically before report generation. Which design accomplishes this?
answers: Have the coordinator evaluate the synthesis for gaps, re-delegate targeted searches, and re-run synthesis.
Let the synthesis subagent spawn its own search subagent directly whenever it finds a thin section.
Have the report generation subagent annotate thin sections as known coverage limitations in the report.
Strengthen the synthesis subagent's prompt to demand thorough, balanced treatment of every subtopic.
feedbacks: This is the iterative refinement loop. The coordinator owns the research plan. It compares the synthesis output against that plan and finds the weak areas. It sends search and analysis subagents narrow queries for only those areas, and then it invokes synthesis again with the larger set of findings. Because the coordinator is the hub, the extra rounds stay visible and limited. The gap is actually filled with new material, instead of being only reworded or flagged.

The Claude Agent SDK does allow a subagent to spawn its own nested subagents, so this is technically possible. But it moves gap-closing out of the control loop that the coordinator owns, and this system depends on that loop. It becomes harder for the coordinator to apply central gap criteria, see which extra searches ran, and limit the number and cost of refinement rounds. Also, the synthesis subagent knows the research plan only to the extent that the coordinator explicitly passed it.

Coverage annotations are the right pattern when sources are really unavailable and the gap cannot be closed, because they make the uncertainty clear to the reader. In this scenario the sources exist, and the team explicitly wants the gaps filled before the report is written. Annotating the problem instead of fixing it does not meet the goal.

The synthesis subagent can only work with the findings it receives. If the search and analysis stages produced little about hydrogen, no amount of prompt emphasis can produce a section with real content. Stronger wording leads the model to add filler or guess instead of citing sourced material, and this breaks the requirement for a cited report.
prompt.explanation:
In a hub-and-spoke research system, each subagent sees only the part of the problem that it was explicitly given. The search subagent cannot know that its hydrogen results were weak compared with the battery results. The synthesis subagent cannot invent findings that it never received. By design, the component that has the whole picture is the coordinator: it has the original topic, the split into subtopics, and the combined results. A subagent could also be given that picture, but only if the coordinator explicitly passes it. So the simplest and most visible place to detect and correct gaps is the coordinator itself. An iterative refinement loop makes this explicit. After synthesis, the coordinator checks the draft against its own plan and finds subtopics with weak support. It delegates new, narrowly targeted searches and document analyses for only those subtopics, and then it invokes synthesis again with the larger set of findings. The loop repeats until coverage meets the quality criteria the coordinator was given. Only then does report generation run.

Two implementation details matter in the Claude Agent SDK. First, a non-fork subagent does not automatically inherit the parent's conversation. So each delegation prompt must state the gap explicitly: which subtopic is weak, what has already been found, and what a sufficient result looks like. The subagent has no other way to learn it. Second, refinement loops need limits. The coordinator should have a maximum number of refinement rounds, and the application should set a spend cap such as max_budget_usd, because every extra round starts more subagent requests that count toward the total cost. Structured output at the synthesis step (for example, a coverage field for each subtopic) makes the coordinator's gap check much more reliable than reading free-form text. See Subagents in the SDK and Structured outputs.

The tempting alternative is to let the synthesis subagent start searches itself. The SDK permits this (by default, subagents can nest several layers deep), and on the surface it seems to close gaps. But it weakens the control loop that the coordinator owns, and this system depends on that loop. Central gap criteria, consistent error handling, visibility into what was searched, and limits on refinement rounds all become harder when synthesis launches searches on its own. Also, the synthesis subagent knows only as much of the research plan as the coordinator chose to pass it. Strengthening the synthesis prompt is probabilistic guidance aimed at the wrong stage. It cannot create cited material that was never retrieved, and it tends to produce padding. Annotating weak sections as coverage limitations is a valid graceful-degradation pattern for sources that are truly unavailable. But it reports the problem instead of solving it, which goes against the stated goal. Anthropic's prompting best practices describe the same cycle: generate, review against criteria, and refine. The workflows documentation shows how to script such repeated rounds across many subagents.

QUESTION: Yesterday a document analysis session named "corpus-review" analyzed 40 source PDFs for an upcoming report. Overnight, a teammate replaced three of those PDFs with corrected versions. How should the team continue the analysis today?
answers: Start a fresh session with no prior context and have the agent re-read all 40 PDFs from scratch.
Resume "corpus-review" and run /compact first so the summary replaces any stale tool results before continuing.
Resume "corpus-review" and open by naming the three replaced PDFs, asking for re-analysis limited to those files.
Resume "corpus-review" and continue synthesis directly, since the restored transcript already holds the analysis of all 40 PDFs.
feedbacks: Starting a new session is the right choice when most earlier tool results are out of date. In this scenario only three of 40 documents changed, and the rest of the analysis is still valid. Re-reading the whole corpus throws away a day of finished work and spends tokens finding results that the session already has.

Compaction summarizes the conversation to free up context. It does not detect changed files or reload their contents. The outdated analysis of the replaced PDFs would just be condensed into the summary. Compaction can also make the exact figures and citations that the report needs less precise.

Resuming restores the earlier conversation, including the analysis of the 37 unchanged documents, so that work does not need to be repeated. Telling the agent which files changed lets it re-read only those three and update its findings. It does not have to guess which earlier tool results are out of date, or explore the whole corpus again.

A resumed session restores earlier messages, tool calls, and tool results, but it does not re-read files from disk on its own. The three replaced PDFs would be represented by outdated analysis. The agent has no sign that anything changed, so the report would be built on old content.
prompt.explanation:
Claude Code sessions are saved conversations tied to a project directory. Resuming one with claude --resume corpus-review restores the earlier messages, tool calls, and tool results. That is why the team does not have to explain yesterday's work again. What resume does not do is check that the files described by those tool results are still current. The transcript is a record of what the agent saw at that time, not a live view of the file system. So any document replaced after the session ended is represented by analysis that is now wrong.

When you continue long-running work, the design decision is whether the earlier context is mostly valid or mostly out of date. When most of it is valid, as in this case with 37 of 40 documents unchanged, the efficient path is to resume and tell the agent what changed. Start the resumed session by naming the specific files that changed, and limit the re-analysis to them. This follows Anthropic's general prompting guidance to reference specific files and limit the investigation. Vague prompts cause Claude to re-read much more than necessary. Referencing the changed files explicitly (for example, with @ mentions) makes Claude read them before it responds, so the updated findings reflect the corrected content. When most results are out of date, the better choice is a new session that starts with a short structured summary of what was found before. This avoids carrying a large amount of outdated tool output.

Each of the other approaches misses part of this. Continuing synthesis directly treats the restored transcript as if it were current, and the agent has no way to know that three documents changed. Note also that Claude Code checkpoints do not record file replacements made outside Claude Code. Checkpoints only track edits made through Claude's own file tools. So the agent cannot discover the change by itself, and the person who resumes the session must say what changed.

In some runs it calls enrich_citations first, producing citations with missing dates. The team needs extract_metadata guaranteed as the first call on every document. Which configuration achieves this?
answers: Set "tool_choice" to the "any" type so the subagent must begin with a tool call rather than text.
Set "strict" to true on the extract_metadata definition so its schema is enforced before other tools run.
Add a system prompt rule stating that metadata extraction must always precede citation enrichment.
Set "tool_choice" to the "tool" type naming extract_metadata on the first request for each document.
feedbacks: The any type guarantees that some tool is called, but Claude still chooses which one, so enrich_citations could still be chosen first. It solves the problem of getting a tool call instead of a text answer. It does not solve the problem of execution order.

Strict tool use makes the inputs of a tool call match its JSON schema. It has no effect on which tool Claude chooses or when. The subagent could still call enrich_citations first, with completely valid inputs.

A prompt instruction is probabilistic guidance. The subagent may still skip or reorder steps in some runs, which is the failure the team has already seen. When a specific first action must be guaranteed, the API-level tool_choice mechanism gives the deterministic control that a prompt cannot give.

Forced tool selection, with the tool type and a tool name, requires Claude to call that specific tool. This is the documented way to guarantee a particular first step before other tools run. The API enforces the selection instead of only suggesting it, so the order holds on every run where forced tool use is supported.
prompt.explanation:
The tool_choice parameter is the API-level control over how Claude selects tools. Its three main settings answer three different questions. The auto type (the default when tools are provided) lets Claude decide whether to call a tool at all or to answer in text. The any type removes the text option: Claude must call one of the provided tools, but it still chooses which one. The tool type, written as an object with a name, removes the choice completely: Claude must call that named tool. Each setting gives Claude less freedom than the one before. The scenario needs the most restrictive setting, because the requirement is not only a tool call but a call to a specific tool at a specific moment.

Forcing extract_metadata on the first request for each document works because the API itself prefills the assistant turn to produce that tool call. So the subagent has no way to start with enrich_citations. This is the documented pattern: force a metadata extraction before enrichment steps, and then return control to auto or any on later turns so the subagent can continue its workflow. Note two limits. First, forced tool use prevents any natural-language text before the tool_use block. If you also want an explanation from the model, use auto with a strong prompt instruction instead. Second, forced modes are not supported in every configuration. For example, manual extended thinking does not accept any or tool. So check the model and settings in use before you depend on it.

Each of the other approaches addresses a related concern. The any type is the correct tool when the risk is a text answer instead of structured output. But it leaves the choice of tool to the model, and that choice is what is going wrong in this scenario. A system prompt rule can increase compliance, but it is still probabilistic. The wrong order that the team has seen shows why that is not enough when a step must be guaranteed. Setting strict to true on a tool definition makes that tool's inputs conform to its schema. It works together with tool_choice but cannot replace it, because it never affects which tool is chosen.

See Define tools for the tool_choice options and forced-tool syntax, and Strict tool use for how schema enforcement differs from tool selection.

QUESTION: The document analysis subagent outputs structured records with claim, quote, source, and publication date fields, and a human currently reviews every record. Overall accuracy measures 97%. What should the team do before removing human review from high-confidence records?
answers: Have the synthesis subagent flag records whose figures look unusual compared to other sources.
Remove review from every record the model rates high-confidence, since 97% already exceeds the target.
Measure accuracy separately by document type and by extracted field before trusting the overall figure.
Add a validation-retry loop so schema violations are corrected before records reach reviewers.
feedbacks: Flagging unusual figures across sources is a useful way to find conflicting statistics, but it does not measure extraction accuracy. It would miss wrong dates, claims attributed to the wrong source, and errors that happen to look plausible. So it cannot show whether a segment is safe to automate.

This treats the overall number and the model's own confidence as enough evidence. Neither has been checked against labeled data for each segment. The model can be confidently wrong on the document types where it performs worst, so review would be removed where it is needed most.

An overall figure of 97% can hide a document type or a specific field that fails much more often, such as publication dates from scanned reports. Measuring accuracy separately by document type and by field shows whether performance is stable everywhere that review would be removed. That is the requirement for safe automation.

A validation-retry loop fixes structural problems, such as missing fields or malformed JSON, and those are not the issue in this question. The 3% of errors are semantic: wrong values in records that have the correct structure. Retries against a schema cannot detect or fix those errors.
prompt.explanation:
An overall accuracy number describes the average across all records. It does not describe the reliability of any part of them. Suppose the document analysis subagent processes clean HTML articles, dense PDFs, and scanned reports. A 97% overall figure can exist together with a 40% error rate on publication dates taken from scanned documents, because those records are a small share of the total. Removing human review based on the overall number would automate the segment that most needs oversight.

Extraction quality has several dimensions. It varies by document type and by field, and automation decisions must be made at that level of detail. Anthropic's evaluation guidance recommends measurable, task-specific criteria that reflect the real mix of inputs and deliberately include edge cases. In this system, that means building a labeled validation set and reporting accuracy for each document type and each field (claim, quote, source, date). Only segments that show stable, high accuracy against that labeled data should move to automated processing. The rest keep human review. A related practice is stratified sampling of records that were approved automatically, so that new error patterns in trusted segments are still detected over time.

Each of the other approaches addresses a different problem. Dropping review for records that the model rates as high-confidence replaces measured accuracy with self-reported confidence. A model is often most confident on the cases it gets wrong, and the confidence signal itself must first be calibrated against labeled data for each segment. A validation-retry loop and JSON schema enforcement fix structural errors. Anthropic's structured outputs feature guarantees that the output matches the schema. It does not guarantee that an extracted date or attribution is factually correct, so it cannot reduce the semantic 3%. Having the synthesis subagent flag unusual figures is a reasonable way to find conflicts between sources. But it does not measure whether extraction is correct, and it would miss values that look plausible but are wrong.

QUESTION: A team is designing the coordinator's control flow. Research requests vary widely: some need only web search, while others require document analysis that then reveals gaps calling for a second search round. How should the coordinator decide which subagent to invoke next?
answers: Add a keyword classifier that maps each request to a predetermined subagent sequence before the run starts.
Prompt the coordinator with the research goal and let it choose each subagent from intermediate results.
Add a PreToolUse hook that rewrites each delegation to the next subagent in a predetermined order.
Hard-code the search, analysis, synthesis, and report subagent calls as a fixed sequence in application code.
feedbacks: A classifier chooses a path once, from the wording of the request, before any research has happened. It cannot react to what document analysis actually finds. So it brings back a decision tree that ignores intermediate results, and those results are the information the coordinator needs.

This is model-driven decision-making. The coordinator reasons over what earlier subagents returned and chooses the next delegation based on the current context. It handles the variation described, including a second search round that happens only when document analysis finds a gap. The team does not have to plan for every path in code.

Hooks are deterministic guardrails for validating, modifying, or blocking tool calls, for example to enforce a policy that must never be skipped. Using a hook to override the coordinator's choice turns the model's reasoning into a fixed pipeline. The system then loses the adaptive behavior that the varied requests need.

A fixed sequence is a workflow with predefined code paths. That is the right choice when every request follows the same predictable steps. The requests in this scenario do not. A fixed pipeline would run unnecessary stages for simple topics, and it could never add the second search round that some topics need.
prompt.explanation:
This question tests the difference between a workflow and an agent. In a workflow, application code directs the model and its tools through predefined paths. In an agent, the model directs its own process and tool use as it goes. Anthropic's guidance is that workflows are better for predictability and consistency on well-defined tasks. Agents fit problems that need flexibility and decisions that depend on what has been learned so far. Open-ended research is the second kind of problem. You can only know whether a second search round is needed after document analysis has run. So the decision must be made at that point in the loop, by something that can read those results.

In the Claude Agent SDK, that something is the coordinator itself. Each subagent is defined with a description, a system prompt, and its own tool access. The coordinator delegates by invoking a subagent, and it receives only the subagent's final message back. The SDK runs the same autonomous loop as Claude Code: evaluate the prompt, request tools, feed the results back, and repeat until there are no more tool calls. So the coordinator can look at the search results it just received, notice a coverage gap, and choose to delegate again. The team's job is to put the goal and quality criteria in the coordinator's prompt and to write subagent descriptions that are clear enough for the coordinator to tell them apart. The team should not script the order of calls.

All the other options take the choice away from the model's reasoning. A hard-coded sequence is a valid pattern, but it is for tasks whose structure never changes. In this scenario it would waste work on simple topics and could not add an unplanned round. A keyword classifier picks a path from the request text before any evidence exists, so it is really a decision tree. A PreToolUse hook is designed to validate, modify, or block individual tool calls as a strict check. Using it to force a fixed order removes the adaptive behavior that the varied requests need. Letting the coordinator choose among the tools it is allowed to use does not affect the real use of hooks, which is to enforce rules that the model must never bypass.

See Building effective agents for the workflow versus agent distinction, Subagents in the SDK for how subagents are defined and delegated to, and Agent loop for how the SDK's loop reacts to tool results.

QUESTION: Asked to trace how citations flow from the search subagent to the report generator in this system's codebase, an agent with Read, Grep, and Glob reads every file under "src/" and exhausts its context. Which TWO instructions correct its exploration strategy? (Select TWO.)
answers: Read every file under the source directory first so nothing is missed before reasoning.
Grep for citation-related identifiers to find likely entry points and call sites.
Read the files Grep returned, then follow their imports to the next files to trace.
Spawn one subagent per source file so each file is read in its own isolated context.
feedbacks: Loading the whole source tree at once is the behavior that already used up the context, so repeating it cannot fix the problem. Read is designed for targeted inspection, with a limit on each call. It is not designed for pulling a whole repository into memory.

Grep searches file contents. That is how an agent finds where citation-related code is without knowing symbol names in advance. The matches give the agent concrete starting points, so it uses context only on files that are relevant to the citation flow.

After Grep has found the relevant files, Read loads only those files, and the imports in them point to the next step in the flow. This repeated cycle of search, read, and follow builds understanding without loading the whole repository.

Starting one subagent per file multiplies the overhead, and no single agent gets the connected view that is needed to trace a flow across files. Anthropic's guidance warns that subagents are often overused for code exploration, where a direct grep call is faster and enough.
prompt.explanation:
Tracing a flow through a codebase is a search problem before it is a reading problem. The built-in Grep tool searches file contents. It is the right way to find where citation-related identifiers, imports, or references appear. This shows the entry points and call sites of the flow, even when the agent does not yet know any specific function name. By default, Grep returns only the matching file paths (its files_with_matches mode). In content mode it can return the matching lines with file names and line numbers. So the agent gets a compact map of the relevant code at a very low context cost. Both results are documented in the Claude Code tools reference.

The agent then uses the Read tool on only the files that Grep found. Each of those files has import statements that name the next modules in the chain. So the agent switches between reading a file and searching for the next symbol or import, and its understanding grows one step at a time. Read is built for this targeted use. A single call returns at most 25,000 tokens, and large files should be read in pages with offset and limit. This is a strong sign that the tool is not meant to load a whole source tree. Anthropic's prompting best practices support the same approach: read the relevant files before answering, and do not speculate about code that has not been opened.

Think of context as a budget. Spend it on the files that matter, in the order that the flow actually passes through them. Reading everything at the start spends the budget according to the directory listing, not according to relevance. That is why the agent in this scenario ran out of space before it traced anything. Starting a subagent for each file splits the picture into pieces instead of connecting it. Each subagent sees one file alone, and no agent holds the trace across files. The prompting guidance specifically notes that subagents are overused for exploration that a direct grep call handles faster. Note that Glob would also be the wrong first step in this case, because it matches file names and paths, not the identifiers inside the files.

answers: Add the server under user scope in the developer's own "~/.claude.json" file.
Document the server's launch command in the project's CLAUDE.md so Claude starts it on demand.
Add the server to the project's ".mcp.json" and tell teammates to ignore its tools for now.
Register the server in ".claude/settings.local.json" since that file stays out of version control.
feedbacks: User-scoped MCP servers are stored in ~/.claude.json. They are private to the developer's account and are never shared through the repository. This is the documented place for personal and experimental servers, so the rest of the team does not see the trial until the developer decides to share it.

CLAUDE.md provides instructions and context that Claude reads at the start of a session. It does not register or launch MCP servers. The server would never connect. Also, because CLAUDE.md is normally committed, the whole team would see the documentation.

.mcp.json is the mechanism for sharing with the team. It is at the project root and is meant to be checked into version control, so every contributor gets the same servers. Putting an untested server there shows its tools to everyone and depends on teammates ignoring them. That is the opposite of an isolated experiment.

The .claude/settings.local.json file holds general project-local Claude Code settings, not MCP server definitions. Anthropic explicitly notes that this terminology is confusing: private MCP server entries are stored in ~/.claude.json. So a server listed in settings.local.json would not be loaded as an MCP server.
prompt.explanation:
Claude Code finds MCP servers through a small set of installation scopes. The scope answers two questions at once: where the server loads, and who else gets it. project scope writes the entry to .mcp.json at the repository root. Anthropic intends this file to be committed, so that every teammate who clones or pulls receives the same tools. user scope writes the entry to ~/.claude.json in the developer's home directory. It keeps the entry private to that account and loads it in every project on the machine. There is also a local scope, which is the default for claude mcp add. It is also stored in ~/.claude.json, but it is tied to the current project path. Both private scopes keep an experiment out of the shared configuration. What matters for this question is that the server does not go into the shared project file.

The design choice is between consistency and isolation. Shared tools that the whole research pipeline depends on belong in .mcp.json. There, ${VAR} expansion lets the team commit the configuration while each machine supplies its own credentials. Untested or personal servers belong in ~/.claude.json. There, they can be added and removed without a commit, without a review, and without surprising a colleague whose web search subagent suddenly sees extra tools. Tools from all connected servers are discovered and offered at the same time. So an untested server in the shared file would also add to every subagent's list of tools, and an oversized tool list like that makes tool selection worse.

The other approaches fail because of how the files work. .claude/settings.local.json is a general settings file, not a place to register MCP servers. Anthropic points out that local-scoped MCP servers are stored in ~/.claude.json, while general project-local settings use .claude/settings.local.json. So a server written there is never connected. CLAUDE.md is read as instructions, not executed as configuration, so documenting a launch command there starts nothing. Asking teammates to ignore tools in a committed .mcp.json defeats the purpose of a private trial, and each of them is still prompted to approve the new server.

When the trial succeeds, sharing it is a deliberate step. Move the entry into .mcp.json with environment-variable placeholders for any token, commit it, and let teammates approve it in their next interactive session. See Connect Claude Code to tools via MCP for the scope reference and Claude Code settings for how ~/.claude.json differs from the settings files.

QUESTION: A teammate suggests letting the document analysis subagent hand its findings straight to the synthesis subagent. Which two design choices keep the system consistent with the hub-and-spoke pattern? (Select TWO.)

Keep error handling in the coordinator so it sees every subagent failure and decides recovery in one place.
Return the analysis results to the coordinator, which includes them explicitly in the synthesis subagent's prompt.
Let the analysis subagent send its findings directly to the synthesis subagent to remove a coordinator hop.
feedbacks: A standard subagent does not receive the parent's conversation history or earlier tool results. It gets its own system prompt plus the prompt string that the coordinator sends. If the design assumes inheritance, the synthesis subagent would run without the search and analysis findings it needs.

Handling failures in one central place is a core responsibility of the coordinator in this topology. When every result and error comes back through one hub, retries, alternative routing, and coverage gap annotations are decided consistently. They are not spread across subagents that cannot see the whole task.

In a hub-and-spoke design, the coordinator controls how information is routed. Each subagent's final report comes back to it, and it decides what the next subagent needs. A default subagent starts with a fresh context. So the coordinator must put the analysis findings directly in the synthesis subagent's prompt, or that subagent will not have them.

Direct transfer from one subagent to another breaks the hub-and-spoke pattern, in which subagents report only to the caller that started them. It would also remove the coordinator's view of what was passed. That makes errors and coverage gaps harder to detect and recover from.
prompt.explanation:
In the Claude Agent SDK, a subagent is a separate agent instance that the main agent starts for a focused subtask. Unless it is a fork of the current conversation, it starts with a fresh context window. It sees its own system prompt and the prompt that the coordinator wrote when invoking it. It does not see the coordinator's history, tool results, or system prompt. Its intermediate tool calls stay inside its own context, and only its final report returns to the parent. This is why the architecture is called hub-and-spoke: every spoke talks only to the hub, and the hub decides what is passed between spokes.

This design is a deliberate tradeoff. Context isolation keeps long search output and document text out of the coordinator's context window, and out of subagents that do not need it. It also makes each delegation reproducible, because everything the subagent knows is visible in the prompt it was given. The cost is that nothing is passed automatically. For the research system, the coordinator must take the document analysis report and write it into the synthesis subagent's prompt, together with the relevant web search findings. It is best to use a structured form that keeps content separate from metadata such as source URLs and dates, so the citations are not lost in the handoff.

The same isolation is what makes centralized error handling work. Every subagent reports back to the coordinator. So the coordinator can tell a timeout apart from a valid empty result, retry a search with a narrower query, send a task to a different subagent, or continue with partial findings and note the gap in the final report. If the analysis subagent sent results directly to synthesis, the coordinator would not see that transfer. If the design relied on inherited history, the synthesis subagent would have no findings at all, because default subagents inherit nothing from the parent conversation.

Anthropic does offer a different mode, agent teams, in which teammates message each other directly and coordinate through a shared task list. It is experimental and separate from ordinary subagent delegation, where the main agent manages all the work. For a coordinator-subagent research system, keep routing and recovery in the hub. See Subagents in the SDK for how subagent context and results flow, and Parallel work approaches for how subagents compare with agent teams and dynamic workflows.

Add a system prompt rule telling the subagent to always prefer MCP tools over built-in ones.
Have the synthesis subagent re-fetch every document after analysis to reconstruct the missing citations.
Add few-shot examples to the subagent prompt showing it calling "fetch_source_document" first.
feedbacks: Tool descriptions are the main signal Claude uses to choose between tools that can do similar things. A one-line description gives the MCP tool no advantage over the familiar built-in Read. Stating the unique source information (source URL and page anchors) that the MCP tool returns, and when to use it instead of Read, removes the overlap at the point where the tool is actually chosen.

A general preference rule in the system prompt is probabilistic guidance. It does not fix the unclear description, so the agent still sees two tools that seem to do the same thing. It also discourages valid uses of Read for files that really are in the workspace.

This adds a workaround later in the pipeline. It repeats work and adds tool calls instead of fixing the tool choice in the analysis subagent. It also moves citation handling to an agent whose role is synthesis, which weakens the role-based tool allocation that the system depends on.

Few-shot examples can reinforce a pattern, but they add tokens, and they do not tell the model why the MCP tool is the right choice. So tool choice stays unreliable on inputs that the examples did not cover. The most effective change for wrong tool choice is to make the description itself clearer.
prompt.explanation:
When two tools can handle the same request, Claude chooses between them almost entirely based on their descriptions. Anthropic's own troubleshooting guidance lists "Claude calls tool A when you wanted tool B" as a symptom that is usually caused by description ambiguity. The recommended fix is to make the tools different by stating when each one should be used, not only what each one does. The description "Retrieves a document" says nothing that Read does not also seem to do. So the agent uses the built-in tool it already knows, and the citation metadata never enters the pipeline.

Agents built on the Claude Agent SDK often prefer built-in tools (Read, Grep) over MCP tools with similar functions. The documented fix is to improve the MCP tool's description with the concrete advantages it offers. In this case those are the source URL and page anchors that the research system needs for cited reports. The description should state that fetch_source_document returns source information that Read cannot, and that it should be used for any source that will be cited. Then the model no longer sees the tools as overlapping, and its choice becomes reliable without any extra mechanisms.

Each of the other approaches leaves the root cause in place. A system prompt rule to prefer MCP tools is probabilistic and too broad, because Read is still the right tool for real workspace files. Few-shot examples add context cost and teach a pattern instead of a reason, so they do not generalize well. Re-fetching documents in the synthesis subagent uses extra tool calls to repair output that should have been correct in the first subagent. It also moves citation work into a subagent whose tools were chosen for a different role. Anthropic describes detailed descriptions as by far the most important factor in tool performance. That is why fixing the description is the first and most effective change whenever the wrong tool is being chosen.

QUESTION: The report-generation subagent needs to replace one of nine identical "Source: pending" markers in a drafted Markdown report, and its Edit call fails because the target text is not unique. Which TWO approaches reliably complete the change? (Select TWO.)
answers: Write just the corrected section and rely on Write to merge it into the existing report.
Retry Edit with an "old_string" that includes enough surrounding lines to match the intended marker only.
Read the full report, then Write the complete contents with only the intended marker changed.
Retry Edit with "replace_all" set to true so the uniqueness requirement no longer blocks the call.
feedbacks: Write creates a file or overwrites it completely. It never appends or merges content. Writing only the corrected part would replace the whole report with that part and destroy the rest of the draft.

Edit performs exact string replacement, and it only requires that the old_string appear once in the file. Adding nearby lines that appear only around the intended marker makes the match unique. The edit then succeeds without rewriting the file.

Reading the whole file and then writing the complete changed version is a reliable fallback when Edit cannot find a unique match. Reading first makes sure the subagent works from the complete current contents before it overwrites the file, and it may be required depending on the model and the file state. Because Write replaces the whole file, the subagent controls which marker changes.

Setting replace_all does skip the uniqueness check, but it changes every occurrence of the string. In this situation only one of the nine markers should change, so replace_all would wrongly change the other eight citation placeholders.
prompt.explanation:
The Edit tool in Claude Code performs literal, exact-match string replacement. It takes an old_string and a new_string, with no regex or fuzzy matching. It requires old_string to occur only once in the file, unless replace_all is set. This strict rule is deliberate. An ambiguous match could corrupt data without anyone noticing, so the tool refuses instead of guessing which occurrence the model meant. Edit is for changing one clearly identified location, and the uniqueness rule is the safety check that protects that change.

When a draft report contains nine identical Source: pending markers, there are two reliable ways to make the change. The first way keeps using Edit but makes the target longer. Include enough of the surrounding lines (the heading or sentence that appears only near the intended marker) so that the old_string matches a single place. This is the fix that the tools reference describes for a non-unique match. The second way is the Read + Write fallback. Load the complete file with Read, build the full desired contents with only one marker changed, and overwrite the file with Write. This approach is less targeted but more certain. It sends the whole file through the context window, but the model fully controls every byte that is written to disk. Reading first is safe, and it may be required depending on the model and the file state. Older models always require reading an existing file before overwriting it, and a file that was earlier read only in part needs a new read. Reading first also guarantees that the agent works from the complete current contents and not from an old copy, which is what makes the overwrite trustworthy.

The replace_all flag solves a different problem. It is for cases where every occurrence really should change, such as renaming an identifier across a file. In this case it would rewrite all nine placeholders, and eight of them would be wrong. Writing only the corrected section is the more dangerous mistake. Write never merges or appends. It replaces the file's contents completely, so a partial section would delete the rest of the draft. The documented rule is that partial changes to an existing file use Edit. Write is for new files, or for complete rewrites that the model has fully built.

In a multi-agent pipeline, the choice also has a context cost. Making the Edit target longer keeps the report-generation subagent's context small. Read + Write loads the full report into context and sends it back out. That is fine for a single report, but note the cost if the subagent handles many large files. See the Claude Code tools reference for the exact behavior of Read, Edit, and Write.

QUESTION: The coordinator receives an open-ended research topic whose relevant subtopics cannot be known in advance. Which two practices should the coordinator apply when decomposing the work? (Select TWO.)
answers: Generate follow-up subtasks from what earlier subagents discover rather than fixing the full task list at the start.
Run an initial broad scoping pass to map the topic's main areas before assigning detailed subagent tasks.
Define the complete list of subagent assignments up front so every run follows the same fixed, reproducible pipeline.
Have each subagent rate its own confidence that its area is covered and re-run only the low scorers.
feedbacks: Dynamic adaptive decomposition means that the coordinator uses each round of findings as input for the next round of assignments. It adds subtasks when a subagent finds an unexpected dependency or area. This is the pattern for investigations whose scope is not known at the start, and it keeps the plan complete as more is learned about the topic.

Mapping the structure first is the documented starting point for open-ended work. A high-level overview shows which areas exist and which are most important before any detailed delegation happens. This directly prevents the failure of a too-narrow decomposition, where the coordinator commits to a few subtopics and misses whole areas.

A fixed pipeline (prompt chaining) is the right choice when the task structure is predictable and all steps are known in advance. For a topic whose subtopics cannot be known ahead of time, fixing the assignment list before anything is discovered guarantees the same coverage gaps on every run.

A subagent's self-rated confidence does not reliably measure actual coverage. Re-running the same assignment cannot find areas that were never assigned. Coverage gaps from a too-narrow decomposition come from the coordinator's plan, so the fix must come from re-planning, not from running the existing tasks again.
prompt.explanation:
Open-ended tasks are the case where dynamic adaptive decomposition works better than a fixed pipeline. The coordinator does not yet know the structure of the problem, so its first job is to learn that structure. It runs a broad scoping pass that maps the main areas of the topic and identifies which areas are most important. Only after that does it produce a prioritized set of subagent assignments. Anthropic's own workflow guidance for unfamiliar codebases follows the same order: start with a high-level overview, and then narrow down to specific components and flows. The same approach applies when the subject is a research topic instead of a repository. See Common workflows.

The second part of the pattern is that the plan must stay open to change as work continues. Each subagent returns its findings to the coordinator, and those findings can reveal dependencies or subtopics that nobody expected. The coordinator then creates new subtasks from that evidence instead of treating the original list as final. Subagents run in isolated context, and only their final results return to the parent. So the coordinator is the only place with the full picture, and that is why re-planning belongs there. See Subagents.

A fixed, reproducible assignment list is a valid design for predictable work, for example a code review that always runs the same passes on each file. But for an unknown topic, it keeps every gap that the first guess contained. Self-rated coverage confidence fails for a different reason. A subagent can only judge the area it was given, so it cannot report on areas that were never assigned. In any case, a model's self-assessment is not a dependable measure of coverage. The exam guide's broader point also applies: when you need an outcome to be guaranteed, prefer checks that can be verified over the model's own claims, as discussed in Best practices.

QUESTION: Logs show the web search and document analysis subagents repeatedly investigate the same subtopics, nearly doubling token usage without broadening the research. Which two changes most effectively reduce this duplication? (Select TWO.)
answers: Have the coordinator state in each delegation prompt which subtopics that subagent must not cover.
Have the coordinator split the topic into distinct subtopics and assign each subagent its own set.
Add a shared log where each subagent records its current focus so the other can avoid it.
Let both subagents cover the full topic, then have the coordinator deduplicate the overlapping findings.
feedbacks: Writing explicit exclusions into each delegation prompt is a second way for the coordinator to set the boundary. A non-fork subagent starts with a fresh context and gets its task from the delegation prompt. So naming the subtopics that it must leave to the other subagent keeps it from moving into the same subtopics, even when the topic naturally leads there.

Dividing the research by subtopic before any delegation happens fixes the root cause, which is unclear task boundaries. Each subagent receives an explicit assignment in its prompt that does not overlap with the other one. The subagents still run in parallel, and the wasted tokens are no longer spent.

A shared focus log asks the subagents to coordinate with each other while they run. This adds custom machinery and a second source of truth that the hub-and-spoke model does not need. Separate scopes that the coordinator sets in the delegation prompt are the simpler and more direct documented way to prevent duplicate work before any tokens are spent.

Removing duplicates afterward takes repeated content out of the report, but it does nothing about the doubled token cost, because both subagents still do the repeated investigation. It treats the symptom in the output instead of the cause in the assignment.
prompt.explanation:
In a coordinator and subagent system, the coordinator decides how the work is divided at the moment it delegates. A non-fork subagent starts in a fresh, isolated context window and gets its assignment from the delegation prompt. So if the coordinator never states a boundary, the subagent is unlikely to respect it. When two subagents are both told, in effect, "research this topic", they will both tend to focus on the same well-known subtopics. This happens even when one works from web results and the other from supplied documents, and the system pays for that work twice.

The documented pattern for parallel research is to start subagents for independent investigations, such as separate areas, modules, or groups of sources, and then let the coordinator combine the findings. The coordinator has to create this independence. There are two ways to do it, and they work well together. One is to divide the topic into distinct subtopics and give each subagent its own part. The other is to write explicit exclusions into each delegation prompt, so a subagent knows which subtopics belong to the other subagent and must be left alone. In both cases, the boundary is set before any tokens are spent, and it is written explicitly into each subagent's prompt. That is why both approaches remove the duplication instead of only hiding it.

Removing duplicate findings after both subagents finish is a tempting shortcut, because it does produce a cleaner report. But by then the token cost of the repeated investigation has already been paid. The coordinator is cleaning up output instead of fixing the assignment. A shared focus log is a different kind of mistake. It moves the coordination problem into the subagents themselves, and into custom machinery outside the delegation step, when the coordinator already controls the division of work directly. Coordination that goes around the coordinator also weakens the single point of observability and error handling that the hub-and-spoke design is meant to provide.

Duplication in a multi-agent system is almost always a decomposition problem, not a synthesis problem. Fix it at the step where the work is divided. See Create custom subagents for the parallel research pattern and context isolation behavior, and Subagents in the SDK for how programmatic subagent definitions and delegation work in Agent SDK applications.

QUESTION: The coordinator session has finished gathering and aggregating findings on a topic, an expensive phase the team does not want to repeat. They now want to try two different report structures from that same aggregated baseline, with neither attempt seeing the other's output. How should they proceed?
answers: Start two fresh sessions and seed each with a hand-written summary of the aggregated findings as the first message.
Resume the coordinator session with "fork_session" enabled twice, giving each report structure its own branch from the baseline.
Resume the session once and ask the coordinator to draft both report structures within the same turn for comparison.
Resume the same session ID twice in sequence, instructing the second run to disregard the first report structure it produced.
feedbacks: A hand-written summary is an incomplete copy of the aggregated findings. Specific figures, sources, and details tend to be lost when findings are condensed. It also requires preparing the baseline twice. Forking carries the complete history into both branches, with no extra gathering cost.

Forking copies the session history into a new session with a different ID and leaves the original unchanged. So each fork inherits the full aggregated findings and then continues on its own. Doing this twice produces two isolated branches that share the baseline. The gathering phase does not run again, and neither attempt sees the other's output.

Producing both structures in one context means that the second draft is generated while the first is already visible, so the two attempts are not independent. It also fills a single context with two full reports, instead of letting each branch develop separately.

Resuming the same session adds to one shared history. So the second attempt would see the first structure in its context, no matter what the instructions say. A model cannot forget selected earlier turns on request, so this does not give the isolation that the team needs.
prompt.explanation:
A Claude Agent SDK session is saved conversation history: the prompt, tool calls, tool results, and responses, written to disk so that an agent can get its earlier context back later. Three operations manage this history. continue picks up the most recent session in the current directory. resume reopens a specific session by ID. Forking creates a completely new session that starts with a copy of the original history and leaves the original unchanged. In Python, you fork at query time with ClaudeAgentOptions(resume=session_id, fork_session=True). In TypeScript, the equivalent is { resume: sessionId, forkSession: true }. The fork gets its own session ID, and the original can still be resumed separately.

This design fits exploration in two different directions. The coordinator's aggregated findings have a real cost: several subagent runs, large tool results, and the coordinator's own work of combining them. Forking twice gives two branches that both inherit that complete baseline, token for token. Then each branch goes its own way with a different report structure. Neither branch ever sees the other, and the original session is still available if the team wants to try a third approach later. This is why forking is better than starting new sessions from a summary, which loses detail and repeats effort. It is also better than working inside one session, where every attempt is added to the same history and contaminates the next one, because the earlier attempt stays in the context.

One limit to keep in mind: a fork branches the conversation history, not the filesystem. If the report-generation step writes files into the same working directory, both branches will see each other's files. Give each branch its own output paths, use file checkpointing when you need edits that can be reverted, or run the branches in separate worktrees when file isolation matters. Note also that the Python fork_session() helper does not copy the original session's file checkpoints into the fork. Claude Code offers the same concept interactively as /branch, and on the command line as --fork-session combined with --resume or --continue.

Read more in Agent SDK Sessions, the Python Agent SDK reference, and Claude Code session management.
